#2802. Colts reportedly still hoping for ‘Christian McCaffrey-esque’ trade package for Jonathan Taylor

According to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport, the Indianapolis Colts remain at a standstill regarding trading their star running back Jonathan Taylor.

The Colts are hoping for a 'Christian McCaffrey-esque' trade capital return to actually move Taylor, which for historical reference, was between the Carolina Panthers and San Francisco 49ers on October 20, 2022, and netted the Panthers the 49ers' following picks: 2023 2nd round, 2o23 third round, 2023 forth round, and 2024 5th round pick:

"Where we're at is essentially where we've been, which is several teams interested in Taylor," said Rapoport on GMFB on Thursday morning.

"Willing to offer a significant pick package, but maybe not quite what Ed Dodds, who is running personnel now in place of Chris Ballard, who was fired, wants, and what the organization wants."

"They want a Christian McCaffrey type package for Jonathan Taylor. It's clear they don't have it yet. Obviously, they would've already made the trade."

"The other part of this thing is, this is not really someone they want to trade. This is someone they believe is a big part of their future. They'd like to build around him. So it would take a big package to get the Colts to move on from him."

There's been some school of thought that the Colts could even be coveting a first round pick to actually part with Taylor, who team owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon potentially considers a major cornerstone of the recently jumpstarted rebuild—regardless of who the next general manager is for the franchise.

That would make a great deal of sense, given that Indianapolis is without its 2027 first round pick, which unfortunately looks like a possible Top 5 pick now and belongs to the New York Jets due to last year's trade deadline Sauce Gardner deal.

At any rate, it doesn't appear as though the Colts ideal asking price has been quite met . . . yet. However, with Indianapolis reportedly holding out until closer to the trade deadline early next week to maximize Taylor's trade return, it's possible a very interested suitor could potentially cave and meet their significant asking price to win the Taylor trade sweepstakes over competitors.

To me, some of this seems like some posturing by the Colts though—although I applaud them for holding out hope of maximizing Taylor trade return until closer to the trade deadline, given they arguably didn't get full trade value return on either DeForest Buckner and Quenton Nelson earlier last week.

Taylor has been one of the Colts best running backs in franchise history, as he's second to only franchise leader Edgerrin James in rushing yards (2,208) and carries (1,699) but is the Horseshoe's all-time leader in rushing touchdowns with 77 respectively.

That being said, he turns 28-years-old in January, and while he's been a great player for the franchise, remains a strong Ring of Honor candidate, and is on a Hall of Fame track, NFL running backs typically do not age gracefully into their early 30's—meaning Taylor may only have 2-3 elite years left. That's realistically the same amount of time it takes to complete a successful rebuild for a franchise—if all actually goes according to plan.

For what it's worth, Rapoport also noted that the Colts are holding out hope for either a 3rd or 4th round pick for starting slot wide receiver Josh Downs, who's a pending free agent that requested a trade from Indianapolis earlier last week and has drawn interest from at least a handful of wideout needy teams.

#2800. Duke Dominates Coastal Carolina in First Half

DURHAM, NORTH CAROLINA - NOVEMBER 02: Deron Rippey Jr. #3 of the Duke Blue Devils dunks the ball during the first half of the game against the Army Black Knights at Cameron Indoor Stadium on November 02, 2026 in Durham, North Carolina. (Photo by Alex Halloway/Getty Images) Getty

DURHAM, NORTH CAROLINA - NOVEMBER 02: Dame Sarr #7 of the Duke Blue Devils reacts after a dunk during the first half of the game against the Army Black Knights at Cameron Indoor Stadium on November 02, 2026 in Durham, North Carolina. (Photo by Alex Halloway/Getty Images) Getty

DURHAM, NORTH CAROLINA - NOVEMBER 02: Patrick Ngongba II #21 of the Duke Blue Devils during the first half of the game against the Army Black Knights at Cameron Indoor Stadium on November 02, 2026 in Durham, North Carolina. (Photo by Alex Halloway/Getty Images) Getty

Duke dominated the first half against Coastal Carolina by a score of 54-18. The Blue Devils were able to get out and run a lot because of their defense. It was the definition of defense leading to offense, and the guards of Coastal Carolina were having trouble bringing the ball up the court. It was a well-rounded first half for Duke, dominated in the paint and got to the free-throw line a bunch.

GettyDURHAM, NORTH CAROLINA – NOVEMBER 02: Deron Rippey Jr. #3 of the Duke Blue Devils dunks the ball during the first half of the game against the Army Black Knights at Cameron Indoor Stadium on November 02, 2026 in Durham, North Carolina. (Photo by Alex Halloway/Getty Images)

Duke dominated the paint in the first half, only making three-pointers. The Blue Devils scored 26 points in the paint and shot 23 free throws, making 17 of them. Their size proved to be too much, and there was nothing that Coastal Carolina could do.

Duke shot 17/30 in the first half, which is 57% from the field. The only thing that they wish they could have done better is not turning the ball over. They finished the first half with 11 turnovers, but they still had a big lead, so it didn't matter as much.

GettyDURHAM, NORTH CAROLINA – NOVEMBER 02: Dame Sarr #7 of the Duke Blue Devils reacts after a dunk during the first half of the game against the Army Black Knights at Cameron Indoor Stadium on November 02, 2026 in Durham, North Carolina. (Photo by Alex Halloway/Getty Images)

The Blue Devils' defense led to a lot of points on the other end. They forced 12 turnovers and had 9 steals that led to 21 points off turnovers and 21 fast-break points. This was a defensive masterclass by Duke, and they didn't give the Chanticleers any breathing room. This was about as good a defensive first half as Jon Sheyer could have asked for.

Even when they weren't forcing turnovers, they were forcing missed shots. Coastal Carolina shot just 6/29 from the field and 2/12 from three. Duke's pressure proved to be too much for them, as they looked uncomfortable the whole first half.

GettyDURHAM, NORTH CAROLINA – NOVEMBER 02: Patrick Ngongba II #21 of the Duke Blue Devils during the first half of the game against the Army Black Knights at Cameron Indoor Stadium on November 02, 2026 in Durham, North Carolina. (Photo by Alex Halloway/Getty Images)

Patrick Ngongba led the way with 18 points on 6/8 shooting and had 8 rebounds. He went 6/10 from the free-throw line and was too much for Coastal Carolina to handle when he caught the ball in the paint. Caleb Foster added 10 points off the bench on 4/4 shooting. Cayden Boozer and Dame Sarr both had seven points each.

Everyone who was in the game was trying to attack the paint every chance they got. They had the size advantage, and it showed. The Blue Devils got good production from everyone who got in the game. It was a dominant first half by Duke, and from the start they overwhelmed Coastal Carolina.

This performance shows how dominant Duke can be and that they don't need to make threes to cause problems. They need to come out in the second half with the same energy and defense. Duke looked really good in the first half and will look to continue their dominance.

#2798. LeBron James is having fun in Philly and one fan's wine can prove it

LeBron James is having fun in Philly and one fan's wine can prove it originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

LeBron James is one of kind in so many ways. What he did Monday night might be the cherry on top.

In the third quarter of the Sixers' 126-107 victory over the Bulls, James decided he'd take fan interaction to a whole new level.

James looked for a transition pass from Tyrese Maxey, who snagged a rebound. James was behind the pass and his momentum took him into the stands, where he disappeared for a few moments.

It wasn't until another angle was shown on replay that we could see what actually went down in the darkness of the seats. James didn't hold back giving reporters a play-by-play.

"I spilled some of his wine," he said postgame. "I crashed into him, spilled some of his wine. So I wanted to see if it was worth it on my arm and how good it was. It was alright."

Troy Clemons – the Sixers fan whose drink spilled – explained his perspective on the interaction with James to Kris Rhim of ESPN.

"[I was] walking to my seat … LeBron crashed into me, he grabbed me, he said 'My bad,' my drink spilled everywhere. He took my drink from me and he basically just took a sip of it, gave it back and ran back on the [court]."

"At the end of the day he's another man like me," Clemons said. "I mean he's LeBron, but at the end of the day, I threw that cup in the trash. And it's nothing up with him, I just got a fresh drink though."

It should be noted that players are not supposed to drink from fans' cups, but it's rare for the NBA to fine someone for a spontaneous interaction such as this. In 2019, a similar thing happened when Mike Scott tumbled into the Bucks' court-side seats. The Sixers star jokingly took a sip of a fan's beverage and the NBA opted not to fine him. Time will tell if James has the same fate.

If nothing else, an interaction like this just shows how much fun James seems to be having.

The 24-year veteran noted the importance of finding joy in the game as he grinds through the season.

"It's a long marathon. And if you don't find ways to have fun throughout it, even though you're working and even though you're locked in, then it could wear on you. So for me, especially at this point in my career, being able to just appreciate the moments, the small moments, these fans are great to us. We try to be great to them as well. By playing the game the right way, playing the game hard and then also just being showmen as well, it was a great game for us."

Head coach Nick Nurse also weighed in on the 41-year-old's mindset coming into the season.

"This summer I think he probably stated publicly that he wanted to go some place and have some fun playing. He loves the game, [it's his] 24th year. It's a group of guys, like I keep saying, that have been super focused in the intent of playing the right way. I think he's a big part of that."

The vibes are high. It's difficult for them not to be.

With Monday's win against the Bulls, the Sixers are 7-1 and lead the Eastern Conference. They've won four in a row and the only team they've lost to is the Pistons. The Sixers will face them on Wednesday to start a three-game road trip.

#2797. Joe Milton on his first start: The NFL is about being ready when your number is called

Joe Milton has never started an NFL game. The closest he came was in Week 18 of the 2024 season when Patriots starter Drake Maye played only three snaps before giving way to Milton, who played the final 61 snaps.

Milton looked like a starting NFL quarterback in that game, completing 22 of 29 passes for 241 yards and a touchdown.

Less than two years later, Milton is on his third team and has played only 51 snaps in four appearances with Dallas since.

He will make his first career start on Sunday when the Eagles play the Giants.

"I was just pretty much going through the plays, going through the week like I was a starter, or like I was playing, and just being ready," Milton said Thursday, via Olivia Reiner of the Philadelphia Inquirer. "And that's what the NFL is about: Just being ready when your name is called, and just preparing for those moments."

The Eagles signed Milton off the Cowboys' practice squad on Oct. 16 after they placed Jalen Hurts on injured reserve due to blood clots. Tanner McKee started the past three games, but went 0-3 as the Eagles ran their losing streak to six games.

Milton has had a crash course in learning the playbook and the terminology, which he said reminds him of the West Coast scheme he had in New England his rookie season.

Milton was asked how much of the Eagles' playbook he knows.

"Shoot, whatever's in this week," he said with a laugh.

#2795. Is Brenton Strange Playing Tonight? Why Jaguars’ TE Has No Catches

Brenton Strange has turned into one of the most reliable tight ends in the NFL.

That hasn't been the case on Thursday Night Football in Week 9 for the Jacksonville Jaguars against the Baltimore Ravens, though.

The Jags got off to a solid start, scoring an early touchdown on the ground with Bhayshul Tuten.

The Jaguars added a field goal later in the first half.

But throughout that, Strange was nowhere to be found.

Yes, the talented tight end Brenton Strange is active and healthy and on the field.

He just hasn't been involved in the action early as Jacksonville works a variety of weapons into the attack.

The Jags connected on a big play to rookie tight end Nate Boerkircher that took a chance at production away from Strange.

They also heavily involved Jakobi Meyers in the early going. Meyers operates in a lot of the same spots of the field as Strange, so that didn't help the TE deliver, either.

Strange has been good for a year-plus, so it's safe to expect him to get some production going. It just hasn't arrived in the first half on Thursday.

Strange wears the number 85 on his jersey, which actually makes him easy to find in the Jags' offense.

All their main pass catchers besides Strange have much lower numbers. Parker Washington is 11, Jakobi Meyers is 3, Brian Thomas Jr. is 7 and Travis Hunter is 12.

Boerkircher, the rookie tight end, wears 87.

The Jaguars have incorporated Boerkircher more in recent weeks.

They drafted him in the second round, and while he was viewed at the time as more of a blocking tight end, you don't draft a player that high and not throw him the football.

The Jaguars have realized that when they throw Boerkircher the ball, good things happen, so they've started to do that more.

It has taken an opportunity away from Strange here and there, although it likely won't eliminate him from the offense entirely.

#2794. Kon Knueppel injury update: Hornets reveal forward has hamstring strain

The Charlotte Hornets seemingly got the exact news they did not want.

Not even six minutes into his regular season debut, Rookie of the Year runner up Kon Knueppel left a game Wednesday, Nov. 4 against the Brooklyn Nets, with what the team then called left leg soreness.

On the latest injury report that published Thursday, Nov. 5, however, the team confirmed that it was a left hamstring strain, which was the same injury that sidelined him for the season's first eight games. The Hornets also already declared Knueppel out for their game Friday, Nov. 6 against the Boston Celtics.

The injury took place midway through the first quarter of Charlotte's game against Brooklyn.

Although there didn't appear to be a specific play in which Knueppel got hurt, he exited shortly after he dribbled the ball off his foot. During the play, Knueppel tried to dribble the ball behind his back but it caromed off his right leg, forcing him to take a small step as he tried to recover it. Immediately after the play, Knueppel limped but tried to stay in the game before quickly heading to the bench. He eventually went into the locker room and did not return.

After the game, Hornets coach Charles Lee told the local broadcast that he did not have an update on Knueppel and said he would be evaluated once the team returned to Charlotte later Wednesday.

Knueppel scored 3 points, all from free throws, missed his only shot attempt – a 3-pointer – and committed 2 turnovers in 5:51 on the floor against the Nets. He did not record any other statistic.

"Hopefully I can contribute in a capacity similar to last year, and with all the offseason work that I put in, even more," Knueppel told the Hornets broadcast in a pregame interview. "It might take me a little bit to get to that full capability, but tonight I'll be ready to go and help us get a win."

Last season, his first in the NBA after the Hornets selected him with the No. 4 overall pick in the 2025 NBA Draft, Knueppel recorded 18.5 points, 5.3 rebounds and 3.4 assists per game. He converted 3-pointers at a 42.5% clip and lost out to his college teammate at Duke, Cooper Flagg, for the Rookie of the Year honor.

#2789. 'We can laugh about it.' Aaron Donald really doesn't want to bumble another fumble

Since coming out of retirement before this season, Rams defensive lineman Aaron Donald adopted a humble approach, always allowing younger, less-accomplished players to go ahead of him during drills.

But on Thursday, the future Hall of Famer enthusiastically moved to the front of the line.

The Rams practiced scooping fumbled footballs off the turf.

"I needed that," Donald said Thursday, chuckling. "Learn bending and getting down."

Last Sunday against the Chargers, Donald missed the opportunity to score his first NFL touchdown when, with a clear shot to the end zone, he failed to come up with a fumble, albeit in hilarious fashion.

"I saw what he was thinking because it's going right in front of you and he's thinking, 'I'm going to scoop and score,'" coach Sean McVay said after the game. "Then he knocks that ... out of bounds. I mean, what the hell?

"His face, he couldn't even look at me and make eye contact after that. But at least we can laugh about it right now."

Donald was still laughing about it Thursday.

"I should have slowed down, but I felt people behind me and I'm like, 'I'm going to get hit in my back. That's going to hurt,'" he said. "So I tried to go full speed and scoop it. I thought the ball was going to bounce this way but it bounced that way, and it just looked all damn silly.

"Then I hit the ball out. I just laid down. 'I can't believe I just did that.'"

Donald was grinning throughout his session with reporters while replaying the missed opportunity — and the new opportunity on the horizon with edge rusher Myles Garrett back at practice.

Read more: Sean McVay's unusual kicker experiment leaves Rams with little margin for error

McVay has not said whether Garrett will be activated from injured reserve and play for the first time since undergoing knee surgery after the season opener.

But Donald sounded as if that could happen Sunday when the Rams play the Washington Commanders in Landover, Md.

Donald did not play in the opener, so whenever Garrett returns would mark the first time the future Hall of Famers will play together.

"If Myles is 100% ready to go, and plays this week, that's going to be amazing for us," Donald said. "It's always good when you have all the pieces of the puzzle."

Donald, a three-time NFL defensive player of the year, and Garrett, a two-time winner, have a combined 236½ sacks. Last season with the Cleveland Browns, Garrett set an NFL season record with 23 sacks.

Donald has played in six games for a team that opened the season as the Super Bowl favorite but is 4-4 after its win over the Chargers.

Read more: NFL Week 9 picks: Bills prevail over Vikings; Packers beat Patriots

Donald does not have a sack, but he has 12 tackles, three for losses.

Will Garrett's return free Donald from double teams and other schemes?

"I'm pretty sure," Donald said. "The guy did have 20-something sacks last year."

Donald said the season has not gone as expected, but he is enjoying it.

"I'm enjoying the process, I'm enjoying myself week in and week out getting better, enjoying being out there with the guys," he said. "And just playing this game."

The Rams activated kicker Joshua Karty to the roster from the practice squad and signed cornerback David Long to the practice squad. The Rams selected Long in the third round of the 2019 draft and he played three-plus seasons before stints with four other teams. ... For the second day in a row, cornerback Trent McDuffie (back), tight end Colby Parkinson (ribs) and safety Kam Curl (foot) did not practice.

#2788. Lakers star Luka Doncic joins LeBron James, issues strong cease and desist

Former Lakers teammates LeBron James and Luka Dončić are fighting a common opponent off of the court.

James is looking to get an AI sports betting app, which is named Bron AI, to stop using his likeness without authorization, a spokesperson for James confirmed to The California Post.

LeBron James #23 of the Philadelphia 76ers looks on during the game against the Chicago Bulls on November 2, 2026 at Xfinity Mobile Arena in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. NBAE via Getty Images

Luka Doncic (77) of the Los Angeles Lakers stands for the national anthem before a game against the Portland Trail Blazers on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

An attorney issued a cease-and-desist letter on the 76ers star's behalf to PlayVision Inc., the sports technology startup that owns Bron AI.

The advertisement for Bron AI that was posted to social media on Wednesday that led to the cease-and-desist shows a person meant to resemble James – wearing a No. 23 basketball jersey with the name "Bron" on it – flipping through the app.

The social media posts amassed over 900,000 views in less than 24 hours before being removed from X/Twitter after Front Office Sports first reported the cease-and-desist.

James, who left the Lakers for the 76ers in free agency this past summer, has an exclusive endorsement deal with Polymarket.

Basketball players Luka Doncic and LeBron James in Lakers jerseys. Los Angeles Times via Getty Images

Adam Mendelsohn, James's longtime media advisor, told The Post that Bron AI's ad is "another example of the decline and lack of originality in sports media."

#2786. Trevor Connelly continues road trip to remember in Golden Knights’ win over Detroit

DETROIT—In a sense, it felt that every move made in the calendar year of 2026 has been preparing for Trevor Connelly to make his impact.

It explains why the Vegas Golden Knights were not willing to make big splashes at the trade deadline last season, and why they were willing to ship Pavel Dorofeyev off to the New York Rangers. While Connelly had struggled with injuries before, he has been absolutely dynamite at every level prior to this season.

What has taken some aback has been how quickly Connelly has found his groove at the NHL level, and this recent road trip through the Eastern Conference has been a perfect example of the rookie being on his game.

In Boston on Nov. 2, Connelly put together a memorable moment by shaking off a first period hit to force overtime with a third period goal. The next night in Pittsburgh, Connelly would again tie the game late to open the door for Tomas Hertl's eventual game-winner in regulation.

On Thursday, the magic continued for Vegas' latest star attraction, as Connelly and the Golden Knights continued to put together an impressive road swing with a 2-1 victory over the Detroit Red Wings.

It took some time for the excitement to start ramping up, however, as both teams were unable to find any dangerous opportunities to get the scoring going.

While the Golden Knights did get themselves into some trouble with their puck management, goaltender Carter Hart was able to make timely saves and keep Detroit from getting on the scoreboard.

However, the dam would finally break in the third period, as a shot bounced off the end boards and directly on the stick of Anton Johansson for the first goal to fall in Detroit's favor.

Just over two minutes later, the Golden Knights would respond with an excellent 200-foot play involving multiple players. Noah Hanifin was able to clear the puck quickly and gave Vegas' forwards an opportunity to move into the offensive zone, eventually giving Braedan Bowman an opportunity to beat Red Wings goaltender Daniil Tarasov up high to level things again.

Then, with just under two minutes remaining, Connelly made magic happen once again.

Entering the offensive zone with the puck on his stick, the rookie was able to make a nifty move to get past a Red Wings defender, then using another as a screen to beat Tarasov on the far side for his third straight game with a third period goal.

Connelly is now once again tied among all NHL rookies with seven goals (Chicago Blackhawks forward Roman Kantserov) and 12 points (Boston Bruins forward James Hagens).

Hart also put together arguably his best goaltending effort of the season, stopping 25 of 26 shots.

Connelly and the Golden Knights will now get an opportunity to come home on a high when the road trip concludes against the Buffalo Sabres on Sunday.

#2785. 76ers' Joel Embiid assessed postgame flagrant 1 foul by NBA for kick to Pistons' Cade Cunningham

Philadelphia 76ers center Joel Embiid was assessed a postgame flagrant foul 1 for kicking Cade Cunningham in the first quarter of Wednesday's 112-106 win over the Detroit Pistons, the league announced on Thursday.

The play in question occurred at the 5:32 mark of the first quarter. With Cunningham defending him at the 3-point line, Embiid kicked out with his right leg on an initial shot attempt before passing to LeBron James. His kick struck Cunningham in the groin, causing the Pistons guard to bend over in pain.

Cunningham was slow to recover as Embiid cut past him for a dunk. He also trailed behind as play went to the other side of the court, grabbing the area that was struck. No foul was called on the play.

Whether it was the pain from the kick or perhaps frustration from no call being made, Cunningham only had nine points in the first half before finishing with 26 (shooting 1-for-9 on 3s) and 11 assists.

During Wednesday's game, Embiid was whistled for a technical foul for shoving Detroit's Tolu Smith under the basket with 1:25 remaining in the first half.

By NBA rules, a player assessed a flagrant foul 1 — defined as "unnecessary contact committed by a player against an opponent" — during the regular season receives one point for the infraction. Accumulating six points results in a one-game suspension. Wednesday's flagrant 1 penalty was the first for Embiid this season.

Two flagrant 1 fouls during a game results in ejection. A flagrant 2 comes with an automatic ejection.

Embiid tallied 26 points and 15 rebounds in the Sixers' win, which improved Philadelphia to 8-1 (4-0 on the road). Jaylen Brown led the 76ers with 30 points, adding 7 rebounds.

#2781. Bears Battling Lions to Trade for $21 Million CB With 12 Career INTs

Cornerback Riq Woolen of the Philadelphia Eagles. Getty

KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - OCTOBER 18: Linebacker Khalil Mack #52 of the Los Angeles Chargers in action during the game against the Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium on October 18, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) Getty

ATLANTA, GEORGIA - OCTOBER 18: General manager Ryan Poles of the Chicago Bears looks on prior to the game against the Atlanta Falcons at Huntington Bank Field on October 18, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) Getty

The Chicago Bears are pursuing cornerback help via the trade market and are currently jostling with the NFC North Division rival Detroit Lions for their DB of choice.

That defensive back is Tariq (Riq) Woolen, currently of the Philadelphia Eagles and formerly a Pro Bowl rookie with the Seattle Seahawks in 2022, who has amassed 59 pass breakups and 12 interceptions across 72 games played.

"Bears might not be done adding to their defense," Thomas R. Petersen reported via X on Thursday, November 5. "They are reportedly in deep competition with Lions to acquire Riq Woolen from the Eagles."

GettyCornerback Riq Woolen of the Philadelphia Eagles.

Petersen's report lines up with what ESPN's Jeremy Fowler had to say on Wednesday about Chicago's interest in improving its secondary.

"The Bears have been linked to edge-rushers such as Khalil Mack, but a few league evaluators told me … that cornerback is becoming more of a need," Fowler reported. "Washington's Mike Sainristil is a name that has circulated this week, though I don't get the sense the Commanders plan to trade him. An available corner such as the Eagles' Riq Woolen for a Day 3 pick could make sense."

It is unclear if Chicago would pass on an opportunity to land Mack, or a similarly-priced and talented pass-rusher, in order to prioritize a cornerback — or vice versa. However, it is possible that the Bears could dig deep enough into their coffers of draft assets and make moves for both.

Woolen is on a one-year deal worth $12 million that expires next spring. He has earned a total of $21 million over the course of his five-year professional career.

GettyOutside linebacker Khalil Mack of the Los Angeles Chargers.

Mack's value is generally falling in the fifth-round pick range, based on the majority of estimates from analysts around the NFL.

But the Los Angeles Chargers (0-7) are sticking firm to their story that they don't want to trade anyone ahead of the deadline, even though literally running the the table from here on out would not guarantee them a wildcard playoff spot in the AFC.

Still, given the Chargers' stated position, as well as Mack's stated interest to remain in L.A. with his teammates, the Bears might need to go up to a fourth-round pick to get a deal done. Chicago surrendered its first-round picks in each of the following two drafts, as well as a 2027 fourth-rounder in return for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons and a 2028 fifth-round selection from the Tennessee Titans.

Chicago now holds the rights to its own second, third, sixth and seventh-round picks in 2027, as well as a fifth-rounder from the Atlanta Falcons, according to Spotrac. That Falcons' fifth is probably the asset the Bears can use to land either Mack or Woolen, who Jacob Infante of Windy City Gridiron also believes is worth a Day 3 asset in trade.

"Given the fact that Woolen is only a one-year rental, it would be surprising to see him cost more than a Day 3 draft pick," Infante wrote on October 23.

GettyGeneral manager Ryan Poles of the Chicago Bears.

The Bears won't part ways with either their second- or third-rounders in 2027 to land Mack or Woolen, both of whom are on the final years of their respective contracts — so it might be one or the other.

However, Chicago holds the rights to its fourth- and fifth-round selections in 2028, as well as a fifth-round pick from the Titans that they got in the Simmons deal. Los Angeles is being as stubborn as they are because they were a perennial playoff team coming into this season (with appearances in 2022, 2024 and 2025) and expected to accomplish the same this year.

But given how much the Chargers still believe in the personnel they've assembled, at least when the majority of those players are healthy, perhaps Chicago might convince Los Angeles to take a fourth-rounder in 2028 for Mack as a longer-term play. In that scenario, the Bears could possibly secure both Mack and Woolen to truly solidify their defense for a possible Super Bowl run.

As 49ers receiver Brandon Aiyuk attempts to lay the foundation for a return to the NFL, at least one other 49ers player has expressed skepticism about Aiyuk’s plan.

#2776. Jaguars-Ravens report card shows a workmanlike effort in all categories

Grading the Jacksonville Jaguars 33-10 victory over Baltimore Ravens on a Thursday Night game in Baltimore.

The Jaguars (6-2) will have a long week before their next game, also on the road, against the Tennessee Titans on Nov. 15.

It was a night when a solid, slightly-above performance was just fine. QB Trevor Lawrence fired a couple of big passes to TE Nate Boerkircher and WR Parker Washington to pave the way to a 17-3 halftime lead. It was nice to see RB Bhayshul Tuten running hard after there was doubt concerning his availability and Ameer Abdullah and Chris Rodriguez helped the Jags control the clock in the second half.

Jaguars coach Liam Coen lamented a bit after the game about leaving points on the field and he was right: the Jags had to settle for Cam Little field goals after getting first downs at the Ravens' 21-, 26-, 27- and 23-yard lines. Travis Hunter got careless with the ball on his only touch of the game, fumbling a short pass away and rookie offensive guard Emmanuel Pregnon had three false start penalties.

With 10 days until the next game, there's plenty of time to iron out those issues.

Everyone from Baltimore to Duuval knew what the Ravens were going to do with an undrafted free-agent rookie quarterback making his first NFL start: try to hammer the Jags with Derrick Henry, who has gorged himself at the buffet line disguised as the Jaguars defense in the past when he played for Tennessee.

That was then. This is now. The Jags never let that strategy get off the ground and Henry had only 57 yards on 11 carries, with 6 yards in the second half. The Jaguars played well against the run (until Justice Hill broke off a 65-yard run against a group of substitutes in the fourth quarter) in their first game without nose tackle DaVon Hamilton and got interceptions from Jourdan Lewis and Montaric Brown.

Fun fact: Hill's TD, with 7:15 left in the game, was the Ravens' first first down of the second half. The Ravens converted on 4 of 14 third downs.

Cam Little made four field goals look routine and he's made 34 of his last 36 attempts in his last 17 games. Punter Logan Cooke averaged a season-high 52.0 yards on three attempts. Jalen McCleod alertly picked up a fumble by LaJohntay Wester on a kickoff return when Wester was initially ruled down.

Coen and the players refused to let this become a trap game, despite all signs pointing in that direction. They were coming off a rout of the Colts, going back on the road, on a short week against a Ravens team that had every reason to fight like wounded animals.

And it was a clean game for the most part. There were only four penalties for 24 yards (three on Pregnon) and the Jags defense responded to the only turnover of the game by the offense when they forced a turnover on downs.

The Jags are 6-2 with 10 days before their next game. That's one game better than they were through eight games last season and they now have a four-game lead in the win column in the AFC South, with a November schedule of the hapless Titans twice and the New York Giants.

#2774. Justin Jefferson says his frustration came from "wanting to win"

Vikings receiver Justin Jefferson engaged in a rare display of frustration late in Sunday’s 19-15 loss to the Lions. He also didn’t talk to reporters after the game, possibly to avoid saying things that would underscore what he was feeling in the moment.

Four days later, Jefferson spoke to the media — and the No. 1 topic was his apparent mood during Minnesota’s first loss of the season.

“It was wanting to win,” Jefferson said, via Kevin Seifert of ESPN, “and I felt like we had plenty of opportunities to win that game and we only hurt ourselves in multiple ways. It’s just wanting better from the whole entire offense especially. And I feel like the potential and the guys that we have in that room is something very, very special. I feel like we’re wasting that if not going out there executing the plays that we have called and just not living to that standard that we feel like we live up to every single day.”

Jefferson, who always says all the right things about his quarterbacks, said all the right things about Kyler Murray, whose performance against Detroit largely contributed to the failure to score more than 15 points.

“I feel like Kyler has continued to grow,” Jefferson said. “I feel like Kyler is continuing to get comfortable with this offense. And I feel like the plays that are there are plays that he’s well capable of making. And those are plays that we’ve seen him make multiple times throughout the season, throughout practice and in training camp as well. So we definitely have faith in him. We have confidence in him to go out there and be that guy that we need him and want him to be.

“But all in all, it’s just executing our plays and just coming ready to play. And I feel like once he’s back out there and he gets more comfortable with the system, more comfortable with just throwing to these different type of receivers, then I feel like he’s going to look a lot better in [reporters’] eyes. But we see that every single day. We see that type of Kyler that we need out there on Sundays every single day. So just bringing that on Sundays. We’re behind him. We’re confident in him, so we just going to keep riding with him.”

For now, the Vikings will ride with Carson Wentz, while Murray is out with a hamstring injury. And Wentz has proven that, of all the quarterbacks who have played for the Vikings since Sam Darnold left for Seattle after the 2024 season, Wentz knows how to get the ball to Jefferson.

Soft bench or not, Wentz has an opportunity to stay on the field if he makes the plays that Murray didn’t on Sunday. Plays that, by the time the game was on the line, coach Kevin O’Connell didn’t allow Murray to try to make.

The one moment that resonates from Sunday’s game wasn’t anything Murray did or failed to do. It came from O’Connell’s decision to punt from the Minnesota 33-yard line on fourth and five with 3:01 to play. Given the manner in which the Lions were running the ball, the likelihood of getting another opportunity to score a touchdown was slim.

Put simply, if O’Connell didn’t trust Murray to gain five yards with the game on the line, O’Connell shouldn’t entrust the starting job to Murray.

For now, Murray technically can’t play due to injury. It’s hard not to wonder whether, if Murray had made the plays needed to outscore the Lions on Sunday, he’d be playing on Monday night despite the injured hamstring.

Per The Athletic's James Boyd, Indianapolis Colts star running back Jonathan Taylor offered a cryptic response when asked whether he has recently requested a trade from the organization, only essentially indicating that "the hay is in the barn now, and he's preparing for the Dallas Cowboys at home":

As recently as last week, Taylor indicated that he hadn't requested a trade from the Colts, despite a few of his (former) teammates such as DeForest Buckner and Josh Downs presumably going down that road as of late.

While it was reported that the Colts haven't been actively shopping Taylor around the league and potentially consider him a cornerstone of their ongoing rebuild to build around and complement, there are a number of heavily interested league suitors, and Indianapolis is clearly listening to prospective offers.

It's been reported that the Colts are hoping for at least a 'Christian McCaffrey-esque draft capital package", and who knows, maybe even a first round pick to recoup some of the value lost from losing their own 2027 first round pick, which is a likely Top 5 pick that now belongs to the New York Jets as part of the surrendered trade package from last year's Sauce Gardner trade deadline deal.

At any rate, Taylor is one of the last key remaining longstanding veteran pillars of the Colts prior regime and remains a Top 5 player at the running back position—albeit an elite player who turns 28-years-old in January and realistically may only have 2-3 prime seasons left at a running back position that isn't forgiving for 30-year-olds.

That may be at best, the amount of time that it takes for the Colts to complete an expedited and successful rebuild (if all goes according to plan) given they don't have a first round pick in 2027, still lack a viable franchise quarterback answer, and the current sad state of their diminished roster collectively (thanks, Chris Ballard!).

There's probably some sentiment for Taylor, who's a strong franchise Ring of Honor candidate some day, remains on a Pro Football Hall of Fame track, and trails only Edgerrin James as the franchise's all-time leading rusher in yards and carries, while already holding the record for most rushing touchdowns in Colts history.

It won't be an easy decision to make either way, unless the Colts are blown away, and it appears as though it may take that type of "king's ransom" running back package for Indianapolis to seriously entertain moving Taylor.

#2770. Messer accounts for 4 TD as Florida Atlantic flies past UTSA, 60-29

Last time Florida Atlantic won six games in a season, the 2020s hadn't even begun. The year was 2019. Lane Kiffin was head coach. And the Owls were still members of Conference USA.

In year two of the Zach Kittley era, that coveted threshold was finally reached. Florida Atlantic secured bowl eligibility with its sixth victory of the season, and it could not have come in more emphatic fashion. The Owls overwhelmed UTSA, which entered the game boasting the American Conference's best overall record at 7-1, in a 60-29 offensive showcase Thursday night.

It marked the fourth 60-point performance in Florida Atlantic history and its second of the season, as the Owls out-gained the red-hot Roadrunners, 563-419.

Wide receiver Easton Messer continued to strengthen his All-American résumé. One week after catching all 16 passes thrown his way for 189 yards and three touchdowns, the receiver delivered another spectacular showing. The nation's receptions leader accounted for Florida Atlantic's first three touchdowns to construct a 21-7 advantage, which included two touchdown receptions and one touchdown pass. That early 14-point lead ensured Florida Atlantic would remain at least one step ahead of the Roadrunners for the remainder of the contest.

Messer's versatility was on full display Thursday. He finished with seven receptions for 85 yards and three touchdowns, added a 14-yard touchdown pass, and chipped in 34 punt return yards and eight rushing yards.

Messer became the first player to record three receiving touchdowns and a passing touchdown in a game since former Washington wide receiver Dante Pettis accomplished the feat in 2016. Over his last three games, Messer has accounted for 12 total touchdowns: eight receiving, two rushing, one passing, and one on a punt return.

His distributor, former Western Kentucky teammate, and best friend Caden Veltkamp may not have filled up the stat sheet to his usual extent, but the star quarterback delivered a remarkably efficient performance. Veltkamp attempted fewer than 30 passes against an FBS opponent for the first time this season, completing 17-of-25 throws for 210 yards and four touchdowns without an interception.

One week ago, Veltkamp attempted 56 passes, tied for the most by any FBS quarterback this season. This time, the air raid offense received its best run support of the season. Florida Atlantic entered the matchup ranked 121st nationally in rushing offense, averaging just 110 yards per game. But against UTSA, the Owls exploded for 339 yards on the ground.

Leonard Farrow captained the attack with a season-high 126 rushing yards, punctuated by a 59-yard touchdown in the late third quarter to extend the lead to 50-29. Ethan Ervin contributed 92 yards, while Kaden Shields-Dutton added 45 yards, as Florida Atlantic repeatedly gashed UTSA for explosive gains.

Florida Atlantic had yet to establish a rushing attack of that magnitude all season, but the offensive fireworks were nothing new for the Owls. The difference Thursday night was what transpired on the opposite side of the ball. Florida Atlantic allowed at least 48 points in each of its last three outings, but the defense brought a different intensity against UTSA.

First, the Owls won the turnover battle 2-0, with Deshaun Batiste and Joseph Sipp Jr. recovering fumbles that were converted into 11 points. Additionally, the Owls thoroughly dominated UTSA's offensive line. Roadrunners quarterback Owen McCown still managed 265 passing yards and three touchdowns, he spent much of the evening under duress. Florida Atlantic repeatedly collapsed the pocket, registering six sacks and 11 tackles for loss. TCU transfer Jonathan Bax spearheaded the effort with a team-high 2.5 sacks.

When Florida Atlantic had a brief offensive lull in the third quarter, the defense stepped up to ensure there would be no UTSA comeback, forcing consecutive punts while the Owls held onto a 43-29 lead. The unit was particularly stingy on third down, limiting the Roadrunners to a 5-of-16 showing.

With both sides of the ball coming together, Florida Atlantic engineered its strongest performance of the season, knocking off UTSA as a touchdown underdog. The Owls improved to 5-0 at home for the first time in program history, with only a Nov. 21 showdown against South Florida standing between them and an unblemished record in Boca Raton.

UTSA (7-2, 4-1 American) suffered its first conference defeat of the season, becoming the last American team to accrue its second overall loss. The Roadrunners entered Thursday sitting just three spots outside the AP Top 25, but their College Football Playoff aspirations took a significant blow in Boca Raton. The defeat also marked UTSA's first loss to Florida Atlantic since 2020.

Florida Atlantic (6-3, 3-2 American) secured bowl eligibility for the first time since 2020 and reached the six-win mark for the first time since 2019. The Owls have averaged 50.7 points per game over their last three outings, signaling that Kittley's offense has hit its stride. But another dimension was added Thursday. Against one of the American's premier contenders, Florida Atlantic showed a glimpse of its potential when the defense matches the firepower of its offense.

#2769. What we learned from the Spurs win over the Mavericks

At some point between the end of the '21 season and the start of the '22 season, I made a pact with myself: no more first quarters.

You have to understand, these were dark times to be a Spurs writer.

And yes, I know, as a fan myself, that those years were no more of picnic for the average fan than they were for me, but still. There's just something about watching a beating and then having to write about it that feels vaguely abusive, especially when some of your favorite people are still involved.

Having to watch Gregg Popovich lose like that…I felt like a journalist covering Muhammad Ali's last fights.

It didn't matter how valiant he was, how much he tried to make something out of nothing — it just seemed kind of dirty to watch at all. We all knew what he was doing, of course.

But watching a worthy sacrifice doesn't make it any easier. I still get misty-eyed when the Iron Giant tells Hogarth Hughes not to follow him (as if he could) before rocketing from the ground into space, and meeting the falling arc of a nuclear warhead.

There's a reason I don't watch the movie all the time. It would be fairly masochistic of me to do so.

But there are 82 games in a season, and someone has to cover them.

As a writing staff, you take some solace in the knowledge that you're all in this together. You're all having to write about it. You're all having to dig for silver linings. And that (for this site) you're all doing it out of some (possibly misplaced) sense of love for the team, and the sport, and the readers who are just about as miserable as you are.

But I just could not watch first quarters anymore. Not in real time.

It's one thing to know that the Titanic is sinking; to be thrown into the middle of the chaos and do your best to make sense of it. It's another thing altogether to watch the ship headed towards the ice-burg in the darkness. To hear the godawful scraping and know what it means. To have been watching the journey for years, and completely run out of ways to spin it.

It had to have been a very conscious decision on James Cameron's part to make that movie a romance. How else could you get people to watch it? The wreck just cannot be the main course.

I couldn't convince myself to watch the game at all if I started with the first quarter. The Spurs would either start taking their beating from the onset, or worse, soar to an early lead that we all knew wouldn't last.

So I decided that I would start watching during the second quarter, finish the game, and then watch the beginning.

It was so much easier to bear when you already knew how it would end. Especially when the Spurs did miraculously pull off the win.

You could go back and break down how the positive momentum started, with the empty but understandable hope that there might be something algorithmic in those 12 minutes that could be reverse-engineered and employed more regularly.

And even the sting of defeat didn't smart as much when you were able to initially avoid the fool's gold of productive opening minutes.

Hell, sometimes it was even a little funny when you encountered the Spurs finding a way to lose the opening frame that you'd never even considered.

(Even though the Spurs won the game, I don't think I'll ever forget Jakob Poeltl picking up 2 fouls in the first 96 seconds of the Lakers game in 2022 that tied Pop with Don Nelson.)

Lately, though, I've been forced to reconsider my first-quarter policy, and the reason is pretty obvious: Victor Wembanyama is just too fun to be put on the back-burner in any capacity.

It was a sensible policy when the losses were piling up. Sometimes it still is.

But frustration with a contender-caliber team starting slowly is simply not enough to deprive myself of the immediacy of the joy provided by the most insane fusion of Hakeem Olajuwon, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, and Wilt Chamberlain imaginable.

Wemby just had the first *official* 50 point, 20 rebound, 8 block game in NBA history (and the first 50/20/10 in the non-assist category if you combine his steals and blocks), in his 8th game of his 4th season, and he's the same age that Wilt was as a rookie!

Chamberlain didn't even peak until he was 25!

That's the territory we're in. That's the conversation.

And that's in spite of existing in the era of injury and rest management. In spite of the fact that Wemby's doing it on a team that's good enough to have already made the Finals.

In spite of playing in an era where blocks are harder to come by, and strategic scouting and game-plans are another level, and players are (pretty successfully) bombing away from long range. In spite of an out-of-whack jumper that's converting at about 28% outside of 10 feet.

Having chugged a 16oz energy drink during my late dinner before the game in an attempt to battle the somnolent rigidities of middle-age, I found myself doing the same 'fighting the urge to pee' dance that my child still breaks out every now and then, as I tried to hold out til the end of the half.

Smelling weakness through the television screen like a shark loose in a blood bank, Wemby proceeded to block three shots in roughly 13 seconds, as if to say: are you sure that you want to miss this?

I can't remember the last time I almost wet myself over basketball, or a more satisfying pee at the half.

There's plenty of negative things I could say about the game. I don't know that I've ever seen this team shoot that badly as a whole. Even Julian Champagnie and Devin Vassell couldn't buy a shot.

There's no reason it should have been that close with such a performance out of Wembanyama.

The bench's defense looked like it had been coordinated by Wile E. Coyote and the Acme Corporation, and they put up a total of ten points in their relief of the starters. Carter Bryant and Tarris Reed somehow got no minutes on a night in which it couldn't have been more clear that a shakeup was needed.

Even De'Aaron Fox's previously next-level show of efficiency took the wrong turn at Albuquerque.

This was a bad game, if we're being honest. A real stinker. And yet I can't find the animosity within me to make this the all-around feel-bad roast that it should be, because, as I've said so many times over the last year, it just did not matter.

This should have been one of those games where I had to go back and break down the first quarter in a state of rage.

It should have been. But I just don't have it in me to despair the undespairing.

Through it all, Wemby was completely unshaken. Understandably, so were his teammates. In their shoes, I think I'd feel the same way.

I don't love that they frittered away lead after lead. I don't like it as a trend, and I don't like it as reminder.

But I think it's easy to forget that we don't live in that place were I can't stand to watch the first quarter anymore, and that by resigning myself to that policy of the past, I'd be getting in the way of my own happiness.

You can't protect yourself from pain without also protecting yourself from rapture. I think sometimes, in both life and basketball, we have a way of forgetting that.

I can tell you everything they did wrong. I can rant and rage with the best of them, and sound my barbaric yawp over the roofs of the world.

I can tell you that they were saved anyway, undeservingly.

Give me a better story than that, I dare you.

I don't have a lot of nice things to say about this game, but man has Wemby really taken to the responsibility of attacking the rim this season. Right now he and Giannis are the only players in the NBA averaging 7+ Rim FGs and 8+ Paint FGs made per game. And Wemby's actually doing it more ways than Giannis is, as the only player in the league averaging 5+ points as the P&R Roll Man, 4+ Points off of Cuts, and 4+ points In Transition, per game. If his jumper starts heating up, we're going to see even crazier numbers than we did last night. Which is insane when you consider that he's 4th in the league in scoring with a jumper finds the bottom of the bucket about 1/4th of time right now.

It's been a bit of an uncomfortable fit for Stephon Castle when all three guards are on the court at the same time, and he seems to have been asked to serve as more of an off-ball shooter because of that, but when the need arises, he always seems to find an extra gear. I know many are hoping that the addition of Tobias Harris forces some rotation adjustments, but I will say, Castle is getting the open shots, and he's not shrinking from the challenge. He's shooting 32% from three now, but if he starts hitting those, that lineup might really morph into something scary, because everything will open up on the inside, and Wemby's already mutilating the rim as it is (and Harper's been slouch, either). And as much as I think Harris will be a boon to the team, I'd secretly prefer to see that happen instead.

Though Fox had probably his most inefficient night of the season on the offensive end, he's still the only player in the NBA creating 15+ Assist Points Per Game, with a 2-1 Assist-to-Turnover Ratio, while also sporting a 65+ True Shooting Percentage, which is crazy when you see all the names that miss the mark. But, just as importantly, he's been outstanding on the defensive end, and it showed in the clutch last night when he kept the still-lethal (and long-time Spurs killer) Kyrie Irving off-balance just enough to that his attempt at a game-winning bucket. To have lost a game with Victor playing like that would have felt catastrophic, so he'd be next in line for the game ball, in my mind.

The Oklahoma City Thunder have a special connection to James Harden, and that relationship produced another memorable moment following Wednesday night's 124-116 victory over the Cleveland Cavaliers.

Harden, who began his NBA career in Oklahoma City, made a point of recognizing injured Thunder star Jalen Williams after the game. The former MVP shared a photo of himself wearing Williams' player-exclusive basketball shoes, accompanied by a personal message.

"It's only right @jalenjdubwilliams PE in Okc! Missed your energy out there champ," Harden wrote on Instagram.

Williams subsequently reposted Harden's message to his Instagram story, adding, "shoutout Uno man !!!"

The exchange carried additional meaning because Harden was drafted third overall by Oklahoma City in 2009. He spent his first three NBA seasons helping establish the Thunder as championship contenders alongside Kevin Durant and Russell Westbrook before being traded to Houston in 2012.

(Photo by Joshua Gateley/Getty Images)

Williams represents a newer generation of Oklahoma City basketball, one that has already delivered a championship of its own.

Although their Thunder careers never overlapped, the connection between Harden and Williams extends beyond their shared organization. Both are Adidas athletes, and Williams has frequently worn player-exclusive editions of Harden's signature sneakers.

Their relationship has also developed into something meaningful away from the court.

In March, Adidas featured both players in a promotional video teasing Williams' eventual signature shoe. Harden even showed Williams a reserved space in his sneaker collection, symbolically welcoming the younger star into the signature footwear business.

Williams later confirmed that his own Adidas signature model was in development.

Wednesday's gesture was particularly fitting because Harden was returning to the city where his NBA journey began. Rather than making his visit exclusively about competing against his former franchise, he used the opportunity to recognize one of Oklahoma City's current stars.

Williams was unavailable for the matchup, meaning the two could not share the court. Nevertheless, Harden made sure his presence was felt through a thoughtful tribute.

(Photo by Kenneth Richmond/Getty Images)

The Cavaliers guard finished with 19 points, nine rebounds and six assists, although Oklahoma City ultimately secured the victory.

For Thunder fans, the exchange offered another reminder of the franchise's remarkable basketball history. Harden helped build Oklahoma City's original championship aspirations, while Williams is helping define its present.

It is not often that two important chapters of a franchise's history intersect through something as simple as a pair of basketball shoes.

But for Harden and Williams, the gesture demonstrated that their connection extends beyond competition, with mutual respect remaining evident even while representing different NBA teams.

#2761. Things aren't unfolding how Aaron Donald and the Rams envisioned

WOODLAND HILLS, Calif. –– A particular kind of silence follows a legend's return.

Narratives write themselves in advance — the final act, the curtain call, the one last ride where the old king straps on the armor and reminds everyone why the kingdom still bears his name.

We, the witnesses, are greedy for that story. We want the coronation. We script it before the first snap and then get offended when reality refuses to read the script.

Aaron Donald has spent half a season watching reality refuse to read the script.

He came back — unretired, un-dusted, un-done — to headline a defense that was supposed to be the counterweight to a star-laden offense.

He came back to play beside Myles Garrett, the man who dropped 22.5 sacks on the league last season, to play with Trent McDuffie and a secondary built like a bank vault.

Donald came back because the vision was beautiful: Donald and Garrett collapsing pockets, the back end locking receivers in a trunk, the whole machine humming, while Matthew Stafford, Puka Nacua and the rest of the fireworks show did their thing on the other side of the ball.

None of it unfolded the way he thought it would.

"I don't got to go into detail as far as that," Donald said.

Something in the way he said it—the shrug in his voice, the laugh hiding underneath—told you the details don't wound him anymore.

"But no, it's not what I expected, but we here. And I'm going to enjoy it though, you know. I'm enjoying the process. I'm enjoying myself week in and week out getting better. I'm enjoying being out there with the guys," Donald said.

There's the headline hiding in plain sight. The man who spent nine years snarling at quarterbacks and answering reporters in clipped, guarded sentences is — at 35, with hands that hurt and a body that aches like a weather report — suddenly the most quotable man in the building.

"You seem a little bit looser than maybe the first time we covered you," a reporter observed, and Donald didn't deny it.

"Maybe I just didn't want to talk to y'all or something. I don't know. Maybe I miss y'all. That's probably what it is, huh," Donald said. "I'm just having fun, man. That's it. Thirty-five years old playing football. It's a kids' game."

Aaron Donald — the most terrifying interior defender of his generation, a man who treated offensive lines like speed bumps — calling football a kids' game with the affection of a father watching from a folding chair.

His fire hasn't gone out; it's just stopped burning him alive.

Something happens to great players when the end comes into view––urgency relaxes into gratitude. The grind becomes the gift.

Donald isn't chasing legacy anymore; legacy is chained to his ankle whether he runs or not.

What's left is the Sunday itself — the pads, the smell, the snap, the small daily miracle that a body held together by tape and stubbornness still answers the bell.

"Ain't what I expected, but I'm enjoying it," Donald said.

If you want to understand the new Aaron Donald, start with Justin Herbert's fumble.

Last week against the Chargers, Wesley Bailey pried the ball loose, and there it was — a defensive tackle's fever dream, a scoop-and-score with nothing but green grass and glory ahead.

Donald's older brother called him afterward: "Man, how you missed your touchdown? We've been talking about that," Donald said.

His retelling of the moment is pure cinema, the kind of story only a man at peace with himself tells on himself this hard.

"I seen a ball. First thing came to my head — touchdown. I'm going to get this ball. I should have slowed down, but I felt people behind me like, I don't want to get hit in my back. That's going to hurt. So I tried to go full speed and scoop it. The ball was going — I thought the ball was going to bounce this way, but it bounced that way. And it just looked all damn silly. And then I hit the ball out and I just laid there. I can't believe I just did that," Donald said.

He lay on the turf, a three-time Defensive Player of the Year, flat on his back, smiling at the heavens, mourning a touchdown that existed only in his imagination.

Stafford, mic'd up, could be heard sympathizing: People don't realize how challenging it is at their age to bend over and get a ball.

Sean McVay texted him that night to joke about it.

"You know, a lot of guys joked about it, and to be honest, I was a little upset with it, you know, because it could have put some more points on the board, at least got the ball back for the offense in the short field. But it's all fun and games because we won. If it was a different situation and we didn't win, it'd be a lot worse," Donald said.

And then, the detail that tells you everything: Donald was at the front of the line during scoop drills this week.

Three Defensive Player of the Year trophies on his shelf, and he's practicing picking up a bouncing football like a rookie trying to make the roster.

"That was my — I needed that. I need that. Learning bending, getting down. So when opportunity presents itself again, I take advantage of it."

Now for the part that stings. Because the vision was never just Donald. The vision was Donald and Garrett — two of the most destructive pass rushers breathing, sharing the same line, splitting the same blocking schemes, forcing offenses to pick their poison and find out both cups are poisoned.

Garrett has been sidelined since Week 1, and the defense Donald came back to anchor has been assembling itself in real time, week by week, like a man rebuilding an engine in his driveway.

The Rams stumbled to a 4-4 start precisely because the grand design kept tearing at the seams.

So when Garrett returned to practice this week, you could hear the exhale across the entire facility.

"It's good to have the pieces back to the puzzle," Donald said. "Was good to see him out there yesterday, today looking good, looking fast. Getting to work with them in full pads and playing off each other — looked pretty good today. I'm excited about having him here, having him back obviously and seeing what he does Sunday."

Jayden Daniels — a mobile quarterback in a season where mobile quarterbacks have been a problem, Josh Allen rumbling for 100-plus rushing yards against this defense a few weeks back, Daniels himself topping 100 against the Giants earlier in the year.

"We got a good game plan. We've been talking about it. Cleaning up some things up front that we can do better — playing off each other, I should say — to not allow him to gash us and hurt us. I'm pretty sure he's going to get a couple plays here and there, but as long as we kind of keep him contained, keep him in the pocket, not let him get them big rush lanes where he can just take advantage of, we'll be fine," Donald said.

The math is delicious, and Donald knows it.

If Garrett is finally, truly back — and "the guy did have 20-something sacks last year," as Donald reminded everyone — then offenses can no longer tilt the entire map toward No. 99. The double-teams have to divide. The protection schemes have to choose a death.

There are a million ways to die; offenses must pick their poison.

"If Miles is 100% ready to go and he plays this week, that's going to be amazing for us. Because it's always good when you got all the pieces to the puzzle out there," Donald said.

The crowning jewel, arriving fashionably late to his own coronation.

Lost in the Garrett noise is what Donald sees behind him — and what he sees, he trusts.

The Rams lost Jaylen Watson for the season with a shoulder injury.

Emmanuel Forbes is stepping into the vacancy.

And when I asked Donald whether he's ever played with a secondary of this caliber — Trent McDuffie, Kam Kitchens and Quentin Lake — he didn't hesitate.

"I played with some good guys, but there's been some playmakers back there that's playing some good ball right now. And obviously when you lose a good player, you got another guy to step up that you trust, and it's always next man up, right? Understanding that the guy that's going to step in, it's not going to be too big of a drop off," Donald said.

Then he reached back, and you could hear the nostalgia braid itself into the present tense.

"It feels good when you got guys on the back end that you can trust. I had some years where I played with some really good football players that played on the back end, where you knew they'd be able to hold the ball a little longer and you get some opportunities to get after the quarterback. And it's like it feels like that again."

Donald doesn't name those years. He doesn't have to.

Every Rams fan who watched the Super Bowl run knows exactly which secondary he's conjuring — the one that let the front four hunt a half-second longer, the one that turned coverage sacks into game-turning plays.

"I think it can be fun. So I'm excited about it. Just ready to go out there and play some ball," Donald said.

Donald won't say everything. That's the tacenda of this season — the unspoken ledger every great player keeps when the plan collapses, and the world starts writing obituaries at 2-4.

He could catalog the injuries, the broken rotations, the games that got away. He chooses not to. Not because the wounds aren't real but because airing them changes nothing, and Aaron Donald has never once confused complaining with competing.

Asked why adversity matters at 4-4, he gave the answer of a man who has stopped negotiating with circumstances.

"There's no way to avoid it. It's going to be ups and downs in a football season. It just happened to happen early. Like I said before, it was nothing to panic about. We just got to keep playing good ball week in and week out, trying to find ways to stay together. Even though the outside world saying whatever they saying, as long as we stay connected inside and we just continue to work through the adversity — because there's no way you can go around it, it's just a part of the game," Donald said.

Stay connected inside; let the outside world talk.

It's the oldest wisdom in football, and it sounds different coming from him now — less like a slogan, more like a man describing how he survived his own expectations.

Because that's the real story here. Not the record. Not the injuries. The metamorphosis. The snarling interior menace of the McVay era has become something rarer and more compelling: a veteran who has made peace with the gap between the vision and the reality, who practices scoop drills at the front of the line, who jokes with reporters he once treated like intruders, who calls a brutal, aching, 35-year-old season a gift.

"You know, from the beginning, nothing played out how I thought it was," Donald said. "You got your vision, you kind of think what can happen. It's like it was a whole 360 of how everything played out for me."

The circle, closing. The man who came back for a coronation discovered the season wasn't about the crown at all — it was about the company. The puzzle, slowly reassembling itself. Garrett on one edge, Donald on the interior, a trusted secondary behind them and a quarterback on Sunday who will find out, probably the hard way, what this defense looks like when the pieces finally all stand in the same frame at once.

"It's never going to be what you expected," Donald said.

Sunday in Washington, the expectation finally matches the reality. For the first time all season, Aaron Donald gets to share a field with Myles Garrett — and if you're Jayden Daniels, reading that sentence should ruin your weekend.

#2760. Brandon Aiyuk to return to 49ers' facility Friday afternoon, reportedly discussing forfeiture of $13 million bonus

Wide receiver Brandon Aiyuk's attempt at an NFL comeback is underway — though it's not entirely clear if or when he'll be able to pull it off.

More than two years after his last NFL snap, Aiyuk is pushing to make his way back, starting by hiring agent Drew Rosenhaus this week. Next up will be trying to make nice with the San Francisco 49ers, resolving a yearlong saga in order to let Aiyuk return to the field.

Rosenhaus told ESPN's Adam Schefter that he and Aiyuk will meet with the team at the 49ers' facility at 3 p.m. on Friday. "We will put our best foot forward and go from there," Rosenhaus told Schefter.

A potential wrinkle in that plan, though, is that Aiyuk owes the team around $13 million in bonus forfeiture as a result of the saga, per The Ringer's Tom Pelissero. The NFL Management Council and NFL Players Association are involved in trying to find a resolution, which could include an agreement to pay the money back, or potential arbitration, per Pelissero.

Aiyuk missed the entire 2025 season with ACL and MCL tears sustained in October 2024. But the real drama began last November, as the 49ers voided the receiver's 2026 contract guarantees after Aiyuk's relationship with the team became increasingly strained when he failed to show up for team rehab sessions and couldn't be reached for contact. In January, San Francisco general manager John Lynch said that Aiyuk had played his last snap with the Niners.

In June, Aiyuk continued to publicly ask the team to cut him so he could sign somewhere else, specifically the Washington Commanders. But that wasn't going to be possible until he was reinstated from the the reserve/left squad, where he landed because he failed to show up for mandatory team activities, including training camp.

In a video, the receiver said that he would never step foot in the 49ers' facility again; he also claimed that he had fired his agent.

Now, with Rosenhaus leading Aiyuk's negotiations, the receiver will hope to finally get his new start elsewhere, assuming the 49ers trade or cut him.

The answer would be that both sides believe they have reached a point of no return; there are no actions left to take, and it's best to part ways with Aiyuk.

You could also include Aiyuk in any potential trade—even as a throw-in in place of a draft pick. You might ask why a team would take a risk on a player who hasn't stepped foot on an NFL field in over two seasons.

#2758. Jones - the smiling wind-up artist who refuses to fade away

An Eddie Jones press conference has always been an event in itself.

You never quite know what is coming. A compliment, a cutting observation, a verbal grenade. Sometimes all three, invariably delivered with that mischievous smile.

Jones belongs to a disappearing generation of coaches who understood that the contest could begin long before the players took the field.

Warren Gatland could intimidate with his imposing presence and gruff demeanour alone. Jose Mourinho proclaimed himself 'The Special One' and made confrontation an art form.

Jones was different. Small in stature, with an almost permanent grin, he could stir up an entire nation while thoroughly enjoying himself.

All three built reputations on dominance. Not simply on the pitch, but over the agenda, their players and the organisations they represented.

But the language of coaching is changing.

Wales head coach Steve Tandy talks about connection and relationships. Brighton manager Fabian Hurzeler emphasises collaboration, trust and understanding the person behind the player.

Neither lacks ambition or authority, but their approach contrasts with the era of the all-powerful head coach.

At 66, Jones remains one of rugby's most fascinating characters from that old school.

In 2018 Jones questioned whether Wales fly-half Rhys Patchell could handle the pressure of playing England at Twickenham, while describing Warren Gatland's team as "confident and cocky".

But his provocations sometimes crossed the line.

That same year Jones apologised after footage emerged of him using some choice language to describe Wales and Ireland in less than flattering terms at a sponsor's event the previous year.

The former was classic Jones. Identify a weakness, plant a seed of doubt and ensure everyone was talking about it. The latter showed when the wind-ups went too far.

Speaking to BBC Sport prior to Japan's Nations Championship meeting with Wales, Jones offered an intriguing explanation.

"Some of them were planned to an extent. Others might have come out of the press conference. Sometimes you say things at the press conference that you don't mean to say. But, yeah, sometimes."

Players picked on form not club location - Tandy

Jones looks to create Japan history in Cardiff

"And particularly with England, I always felt with the English that they didn't have enough confidence in themselves."

Jones explained that part of his responsibility was to provide that self-belief.

"So I felt one of my roles was to give them that confidence, to be almost the battering ram for them."

For Jones, the mind games served more than one purpose. Unsettling opponents was one thing, but taking pressure off his players was just as important.

And if that meant making himself the centre of attention, so be it.

An extraordinary workaholic, he is renowned for his almost impossible standards. Players have described receiving messages from him at 3am while he was exercising, only to be questioned at breakfast about why they had not replied.

Yet even as an international coach, Jones has been known to quietly turn up at local clubs to coach minis, or drive hours to a player's testimonial dinner without a fee.

His career has had its extremes. England dismissed him in 2022, while his return to Australia ended with the Wallabies' first pool-stage exit at the 2023 World Cup.

In Lyon, after Australia had been thrashed by Wales, the familiar grin was absent. Jones was prickly, irritated and facing questions about his future.

Three years on, as he looked forward to Japan facing Wales in Cardiff in the Nations Championship on Saturday, the contrast was striking. Relaxed, charming and generous with his answers, he appeared to be thoroughly enjoying himself.

Born in Australia with a Japanese mother, Eddie Jones has had two spells as Japan head coach [Getty Images]

For all his contradictions, Jones remains a rugby obsessive. Nothing illustrated that better than his answer when asked which Welsh player had left the greatest impression on him.

Not Gareth Edwards, Shane Williams or Alun Wyn Jones, but Liam Williams, the former Wales and British and Irish Lions full-back renowned for his bravery under the high ball.

"Every time I come to Millennium Stadium (sic), I have this picture of Liam Williams winning box kicks," Jones told the Scrum V podcast.

"He was all elbows and knees, but he could do something brilliant in the game."

It was a rugby purist's answer. An appreciation of the finer details rather than simply the most celebrated names.

That affection for the finer details extends to Welsh rugby more broadly.

Jones spoke warmly of Cardiff's Principality Stadium and praised Steve Tandy's rebuilding work, particularly the leadership of Dewi Lake and Jac Morgan.

But the old competitive instincts remain.

Japan's coach knows the value of silencing the Cardiff crowd, and believes a strong start could turn Welsh supporters' frustrations into a psychological advantage.

Even the charming, reflective Jones is still searching for an edge.

As the conversation ended, he offered encouragement to Welsh supporters.

"So, yeah, for the Welsh supporters, just keep backing your team."

"But don't back them too much on Saturday."

Wales opt for centre power pair against Japan

Where are Wales internationals really made?
