#2757. Game Preview #10: Wolves at Pelicans Game Thread

Fresh off of a tough win against a talented Houston Rockets squad, the Minnesota Timberwolves take on Zion Williamson and the New Orleans Pelicans on Friday night.

Who: Minnesota Timberwolves (6-3) vs New Orleans Pelicans (4-4)

Where: Smoothie King Center — New Orleans, LA

After starting the year 0-4, the Pelicans have ripped off four straight wins to claw back to .500. Sprinkled into that winning streak are some impressive victories over the surging Memphis Grizzlies (handing them their only loss on the season thus far) and the Atlanta Hawks. New Orleans is not a squad that is projected to climb the Western Conference standings or necessarily strike fear in the hearts of opponents, though they are still a team with enough competitive and ascending players to keep opponents honest.

Considering the still shorthanded state of the Wolves, they may have their hands full with a healthy-for-now Pelicans team. The win over the Rockets was thoroughly impressive, though Chris Finch and company will need to remain focused if they are to come out of this game with a victory.

Here are a few things I am looking out for against New Orleans:

You know the guys – the dudes who love to turn up and have career games against the Wolves no matter what state their team is in. Most teams in the NBA have at least one Wolf Killer. The Pelicans have a few.

Perhaps most obvious of these players is Zion Williamson, who averages a whopping 28.5 points per game against Minnesota, nearly five points higher than his career average of 23.8. When healthy, Williamson is one of the premier tickets in the league and can score at will against nearly anyone. Jonathan Kuminga and Rudy Gobert will have their hands full with Zion, who will seek to outmuscle and overpower anyone that Finch decides to throw at him.

Saddiq Bey is another player that ramps up his production against the Timberwolves. A career 14.8 ppg scorer, his number increases to 19.5 for his career against Minnesota. As a member of the Pelicans, Bey's average jumps up to 24 ppg versus the Wolves. The guy just flat out doesn't like us.

As the Pelicans have other surging young players contributing to their recent run of success, this matchup may be more difficult than initially expected. Derik Queen has looked to be a solid NBA big man and Jeremiah Fears has been becoming a more well-rounded player. If Minnesota's defenders can keep the Wolf Killers from transforming into much better versions of themselves, the game is there for the taking.

Bones Hyland is a fun player. He's energetic, has a great smile, and keeps the fanbase engaged with his aesthetically pleasing style of play and affable three-point shot celebration. He's an ideal bench player that could fit in on many teams. We are fortunate to have him as a Timberwolf.

However, with a slew of injuries that continue to hamper Minnesota's preferred personnel, Bones continues to be thrust into heavier minutes than he would normally get. In the four games before Anthony Edwards got injured, Hyland played an average of eight minutes per night. Since then, his minutes have doubled, playing 16 minutes per game in the five matchups since Edwards (and now Terrence Shannon Jr.) went down.

Bones's 19 point, eight assist night against the Los Angeles Clippers last week was a true representation of what he can bring as a player when he's on. It's unrealistic to expect that kind of production and efficiency from him most nights, though he does help the Timberwolves find tempo and form whenever things are going south.

If the Timberwolves are going to have any sustained success while Edwards and TSJ are out, Hyland will need to continue to exert efficiency and production in his limited time on the court. He was electric against the Rockets, scoring 19 points in just 16 minutes of play. For a team that continues to lose players at a high clip, Bones will remain an integral part of the offensive flow moving forward.

There's not much more that can be said about just how putrid Minnesota's free throw shooting has been. Currently the team sits at 63.4%, good for dead last and a massive 7% behind the next closest team, which is the 1-7 Milwaukee Bucks. Minnesota shot a cool 53% (10-19) at the line just last night versus Houston in a 10-point victory to bring that percentage down even lower. So it goes.

It's not like this team has a problem shooting the ball, either. That's what makes this ineptitude so baffling. The Timberwolves shot 53% from the floor and 43% from distance against the Rockets. And yet, while standing at the free throw line, uncontested and still, they can't put the ball in the hoop.

Two players on the Wolves are shooting greater than 80% from the line this season. Everyone else is below them. That is unacceptable.

It would appear that Gobert's inability to consistently make shots from the charity stripe (42.6% on nearly six attempts per game) is becoming contagious to the rest of the team. While it hasn't been the biggest issue the Timberwolves have faced this season, it will become one as the team enters more late-game clutch time situations. We're not far off from a few tight losses spurring a dialogue that laments the team's lack of efficiency from the line. The recent defeat at the hands of the Golden State Warriors comes to mind, poor officiating be damned.

Chris Finch will need to address this problem somehow. Unfortunately, getting reps from the free throw line will not show itself as immediately game-changing. It will take time. Finishing this season anywhere but dead last should be seen as a success at this point. Until then, Minnesota needs to figure out how to capitalize on the opportunities they are given.

#2755. Will Arch Manning, Dante Moore and other QB prospect questions influence NFL trade deadline?

As Tuesday's NFL trade deadline draws closer, front offices at all 32 teams are asking themselves: How much do we value our coming draft picks?

And how does that value compare to our assessment of this year's trade candidates?

The question circulates every year. But with a 2027 NFL Draft class that was strongly heralded in the spring, the calculus feels different.

"Last year, the '27 draft was looming over the '26 draft far more than usual," said a league source with a long history of evaluating the NFL Draft and its quarterback landscape, speaking on condition of anonymity in order to speak freely. "And it has not been a stellar year."

In particular, the first half of the 2026 college football season has not raised the NFL's excitement level about the quarterback class that awaits. Fair or not, that buzz tends to influence the perception of the entire class.

So while talent evaluations between now and April could still shift, it's worth asking: Will a shift in perception of the coming quarterback class influence the NFL trade deadline next week?

Texas QB Arch Manning has cast doubt on his NFL draft potential with his inconsistent play for the Longhorns this season.

In April, teams were wary of trading away 2027 picks due to the buzz around the class, which stemmed largely from buzz around the crop of potential first-round quarterbacks. If the hype has dimmed, are those picks more for sale?

Like most trends in the NFL, the philosophy will differ from team to team. But conversations with league and team voices acknowledge that some draft-eligible players are losing their shine, and some teams could parlay that belief into feeling emboldened at the deadline to acquire players at positions they may not feel the draft is guaranteed to deliver.

Information on draft prospects is incomplete by early November. But one high-ranking AFC executive said they could already get a general sense of the deeper and shallower areas of the draft even if individual evaluations remain unfinished.

"You have all the information, you have general medical history and then you have early background and you can kind of form [opinions]," one high-ranking AFC executive told Yahoo Sports. "You can get close enough to where it's like, 'OK, it's deep. We can solve that in the draft.' Or you're blending with the draft from free agency where it's like [a position] is weaker than other years based on our information [so] it probably makes sense to make this move because between now and the draft, we probably can't solve it the way we want to solve it if we don't do this.

"You're trying to use all that information to piece together the plan."

What information will teams across the league be piecing together? Here's what Yahoo Sports is hearing.

Conversations with executives and evaluators across six different teams offered a mosaic of opinions.

Evaluators from two AFC teams and a high-ranking executive from an NFC team each confirmed they do not view the 2027 NFL Draft as highly now as they did this summer. Each said that reflected their current evaluations of the quarterback class.

"I was part of [the hype], too," one AFC evaluator said. "I got caught up, probably told a bunch of people how this is going to be one of the best draft classes in a long time and it's turning out [not] to be. … There's some good players and there's some really good players at the top, like [Ohio State receiver] Jeremiah Smith. There's a few other players that are really, really talented, but they have a lot of baggage. …

"But this draft isn't turning out to be as deep and as loaded as I anticipated and hoped."

The evaluator from the other AFC team said they believe that 75-80% of draft classes are similarly talented, but perceptions of elite players at premium positions — quarterback, receiver, edge rusher and offensive tackle — disproportionately shift perceptions of each draft. This year, the evaluator saw a dip in receiver, edge and quarterback certainty.

"If that's the case, it's worth buying a player that you can get control on rather than waiting and guessing at the draft," an NFC executive said. "I do think that's part of the Texans' thesis with Marvin Harrison."

Quarterback questions from evaluators rage: Is Mississippi's 6-foot Trinidad Chambliss big enough for the league? Will Miami's Darian Mensah have faced tough enough defenses to predict his pro success accurately? Are college defensive coordinators overwhelmingly cracking the code on college quarterbacks more effectively?

The two biggest question marks at quarterback this season stem from Texas quarterback Arch Manning and Oregon quarterback Dante Moore. Manning has proven inconsistent through eight games, including in pivotal moments. Moore's season ended Sept. 26 after he suffered a concussion. Questions on each player weigh their readiness for the NFL and their interest in declaring pro this spring rather than exploring another college year.

Evaluators are split on whether a transfer would help Manning find a better offensive fit. One camp believes that would be the fresh start he needs, while the other believes his family pedigree and résumé will already net him first-round consideration so having just one year to adjust to a new system alongside new teammates could end up hurting his stock more than helping it. Moore, meanwhile, could help his stock if he shows a cleaner bill of health and gets more than his current limited sample size of 19 college starts, evaluators said.

Several quarterbacks are still expected to be drafted in the first round, including the season's biggest riser to this point in Oklahoma State's Drew Mestemaker. One AFC evaluator said Mestemaker, Notre Dame's CJ Carr and Mensah each would have earned higher evaluations than 2026 first overall pick Fernando Mendoza. Chambliss and Missouri's Austin Simmons intrigue evaluators as well.

Even with mixed reviews on premium positions, including quarterback, a high-ranking AFC executive and a high-ranking NFC executive agreed the draft has more consensus high-end talent than the 2026 class.

"I would say this [year] is maybe a little deeper than last year's in the top 15-20 picks in other positions than quarterback," the high-ranking NFC executive said. "But then after that, it seems like it's a little leaner, and the drafts have been getting a little leaner."

The high-ranking AFC executive credited last year's offensive tackle class and a handful of elite players, like Giants linebacker Arvell Reese. The executive wondered: Are quarterbacks shifting the perception too much?

"The quarterback class, I think people just keep overcorrecting," the executive said. "I think they overcorrected high and now they're overcorrecting all these guys can't play, they'll all stay in school.

"A lot of the sentiment on the draft is driven by what people think about the QBs. But I think even if you take them out, there's some really, really high-end dudes in this draft."

Evaluators and executives were split on how much the coming draft truly influences teams' trade deadline strategies.

Some evaluators and executives emphasized building a roster is a holistic process that constantly requires a multiyear vision integrating the trade deadline, free agency and draft.

Others believed trade-deadline acquisitions, and their often steep costs, prioritize the current season's outlook. A league source considered teams in three categories.

"There's a team that they're not going to get in the playoffs and so they're doing the best they can to build a winning culture and they're basically playing for next year," the source said of the first group. "Then you have a group of teams that they can get in the playoffs, but they can't win in the playoffs. …

"Then you get teams [that], hey, get in the playoffs and anything can happen."

Expect teams like the Buffalo Bills, Kansas City Chiefs and Chicago Bears (Jeffery Simmons already, but perhaps more?) to buy, capitalizing on their already-high ceilings.

Expect teams like the Minnesota Vikings, Pittsburgh Steelers and Seattle Seahawks (like the Bears, they've already started) to assess whether they can narrow the gap on rosters that simultaneously hold glaring weaknesses and playoff-caliber strengths.

And then expect teams like the Indianapolis Colts (in progress), Tennessee Titans (in progress, via Simmons trade) and perhaps even the Las Vegas Raiders to recognize that accumulating assets for next year and beyond is more valuable.

That trifecta should guide teams making bigger swings, the league source said. A high-ranking AFC executive believed there was more nuance involved.

"Honestly, every team in each segment has an argument to make a trade," the executive said. "It's just the level."

Players with potential to meaningfully impact a team beyond 2026 could attract suitors from different competitive stages. Expensive players at depreciating positions (looking at you, Jonathan Taylor) make less sense for teams that aren't contending this season.

Whether teams have a scarcity mindset around draft picks could unfold similarly: Teams like the Titans, New York Jets and Los Angeles Chargers would have little reason to send off their first-round pick as they struggle to win games. But sending a mid-round pick for a player on an expiring deal? Those decisions are more record- and draft class-agnostic, some believe.

"I don't think people care when they trade a third or a fourth," an AFC talent evaluator said. "They look at those as pretty stable resources year over year.

"But I think the teams maybe that are at the top of the draft would maybe consider it because you can kind of anticipate those spots by what's going to be available."

Arguably the most important caveat in any of these decisions: accurately assessing a team's place in its competitive and resource-allocation lifecycle. Trades bust most when teams overestimate their readiness, as the Colts did last year when trading two first-round picks for cornerback Sauce Gardner and the Atlanta Falcons traded back into the first round of the 2025 NFL Draft for edge rusher James Pearce Jr. In contrast, a Bears team that won two of three games even without Caleb Williams this year gave counterparts more confidence in its logic to send two first-rounders for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons.

"The teams that do the best job on these trades [are] really understanding what phase you're in and stacking it," the AFC talent evaluator said. "Seattle has a loaded roster and one elite guard really helped them. The Jets have tons of draft capital so acquiring picks makes sense. When you cherry-pick and only do one here and there, I don't think you really get the value or help your franchise long term.

"It's really just a constant balance and a constant push and pull of trying to identify where your team is and what you're going to be in a year or two years because that's where it becomes really valuable."

#2754. 2026-27 NHL season predictions: Expert picks for Stanley Cup playoffs, champion and major awards this season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Following a brief offseason and an expedited preseason, the 2026-27 NHL season has arrived. Before the puck drops on opening night, we have some predictions to make.

If this season feel like it's staring earlier than usual, that's because it is. The NHL is adopting an 84-game regular season, which just means more hockey for the rest of us. That also means a long and arduous journey to the Stanley Cup is ever so slightly more difficult.

So, what will that journey look like? The Carolina Hurricanes are looking to defend their title as Cup champions, but they'll have to contend with a deep Eastern Conference and some real juggernauts in the Western Conference. With that in mind, we logged our expert predictions for the playoff field in each conference -- and there were a few surprises -- before making our Stanley Cup Final selections.

We also called our shot on the winners of each major individual award. Connor McDavid is looking for his fourth Hart Trophy, but he's got some competition from an up-and-coming superstar in his own division. Races for the Norris Trophy and Vezina Trophy should be pretty wide open, and unexpected candidates always emerge throughout the season.

It should be a fun season in the NHL, so follow along with all our coverage at CBS Sports. Let's get things kicked off with the season preview and predictions, which will of course be 100% accurate.

Baumgartner: I don't see many new faces entering the conversation when it comes to the Eastern Conference playoff race. A healthy Florida Panthers side will slot themselves right back towards the top of the Atlantic, and a revamped Washington Capitals side should be able to make some noise in the Metropolitan. Besides that, I have six 2026 playoff teams returning to the dance in 2027.

Nivison: As much as I hate to go with chalk in preseason predictions -- because it rarely happens that way -- there's no denying the top dogs in the West. The Avalanche and Stars are the class of the Central Division, and the Golden Knights should pound a pitiful Pacific Division into a pulp. Things get more interesting behind those clear Cup contenders, and I'm projecting another significant leap forward from the Mammoth. I also think Macklin Celebrini will be successful in dragging the Sharks to the playoffs in his third NHL season.

Nivison -- Columbus Blue Jackets: The Blue Jackets have been agonizingly close to the playoffs in each of the last two seasons, and I think they get over the hump in 2026-27. There are still questions in Columbus. Can Adam Fantilli be a franchise player at center? Is the forward group as a whole good enough to keep pace in a competitive Eastern Conference? Still, I am sure the Blue Jackets have a really strong blue line, led by Norris Trophy winner Zach Werenski, and goaltender Jet Greaves is on track to become a Vezina Trophy candidate. Internal improvements from the young core will then get Columbus above the cut line.

Baumgartner -- San Jose Sharks: The Sharks narrowly missed out on the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, finishing just four points short of the second wild card. San Jose added a good group of veterans over the summer, but the most important offseason move was selecting Ivar Stenberg with the No. 2 pick in the Draft. Stenberg joins the youth movement in San Jose, which is spearheaded by new captain Macklin Celebrini, who broke the Sharks single-season points record with 115 last season. The Sharks are a better team than they were last year, and with Celebrini entering his third season as a legit Hart Trophy contender, this team won't be fun to play against.

Nivison: Yes, the Mammoth have a brutal path coming out of the Central Divison, but just close your eyes and imagine this scenario with me. Logan Cooley becomes a superstar center. Dylan Guenther hits 50 goals. Dmitry Simashev asserts himself as a budding top-four defenseman. Anders Lee and Vincent Trocheck provide necessary veteran depth. Now open your eyes. Utah is your Western Conference champion.

Unfortunately for the Mammoth, they will run into a refreshed Panthers team that now has double-barreled Tkachuks. Last season, we found out that all it takes to stop Florida is to hope all of its key players miss significant time with injury. The long offseason was probably a blessing in disguise as it allowed the Panthers to get healthy, and that's bad news for everyone else. The structure in front of the crease will limit some of the volatility we saw from Jacob Markstrom in New Jersey, and Florida wins its third Stanley Cup in four years.

Baumgartner: Before last season, the Carolina Hurricanes' kryptonite was the Eastern Conference Final. The Hurricanes were able to overcome their demons and win the East before ultimately taking home the franchise's first Stanley Cup since 2006. In the West, the Dallas Stars have been running into the same problem. After three straight seasons ending in the Western Conference Final, the Stars regressed last postseason, flaming out in the first-round to the Minnesota Wild. The Central Division will once again be a gauntlet, but I'm ready for Dallas to take the next step and reach the Stanley Cup Final.

While Dallas has continued to fall short in recent years, the Panthers have done the opposite. The Panthers made three consecutive Stanley Cup Final appearances, winning back-to-back Cups in 2023-24 and 2024-25. Last season, Florida's three-peat attempt came to a halt on day one of training after captain Aleksander Barkov went down with a non-contact injury, tearing both the ACL and MCL in his right knee. An offseason of healing for Barkov, and the rest of the banged up Panthers, has the team refreshed entering September for the first time in years. With nearly the entire 2025 Stanley Cup winning core still on the team and Brady Tkachuk added to the fold, Florida looks ready to win its third Stanley Cup in four seasons.

Nivison: Celebrini should have won the Hart Trophy last season, but for some incomprehensible reason, he wasn't even a finalist. This year, Celebrini replicates that performance and gets San Jose to the postseason to take home his first MVP award at age 20. Hughes posts a career year in his first full season with the Wild, and Spencer Carberry gets his flowers for winning the Metro Division after missing the playoffs last year.

Baumgartner: McDavid's ability to take over a game was evident nearly every time he touched the ice last season. His 24 points (11 goals,13 assists) in the final 14 games of the regular season -- without Leon Draisaitl in the lineup -- was one of the many reasons I put him No. 1 on my Hart Trophy ballot. With just two years left on his current contract, desperation may start to kick in to get the job in Edmonton, which would lead to another MVP-caliber season. Barkov is healthy and the frontrunner to win his fourth Selke, and Dahlin will have another strong season to take home his first career Norris Trophy.

#2752. 4 things to watch as the Mavericks’ Cup quest continues against the Utah Jazz

The Dallas Mavericks (4-4) will meet the Utah Jazz (1-7) 7:00pm CST Friday at American Airlines Center in the the group stage of the in-season NBA Cup tournament. Dallas enters this contest on a two-game slide after their comeback attempt Wednesday against San Antonio came up short, 112-111. After a challenging stretch of the schedule to begin the season, the Mavericks face their second opponent this week to bring a record with fewer than two wins into the AAC; Monday the Sacramento Kings improved to 1-6 against a Mavericks team without Kyrie Irving, 115-100. The Jazz arrive having dropped six straight after the Pelicans prevailed Wednesday in overtime, 120-113. The Mavericks and Jazz share a common opponent this week, as Jazz fell Monday to the Spurs, 119-97.

The Jazz organization's goals remain more focused on developing their young core than immediate playoff contention, but in dealing for forward Jaren Jackson Jr. last spring, CEO Danny Ainge moved beyond the rebuilding phase of angling for draft position with a trade that greatly bolstered the team's chances (and expectations) of winning now. Jackson's departure against the Grizzlies Oct. 26 with a torn MCL means that the team will turn to the stockpile of talent amassed in recent drafts, like forward Ace Bailey, guard Darryn Peterson, and point guard Keyonte George.

All three of those players seem to have bright futures, but it is Lewisville's George who has emerged as the most NBA-ready player as of this writing. The big guard hit some big shots against New Orleans Wednesday, icing a jumper that seemed to have won it before replays revealed that the ball left his hands a split second late, then knocking down the first six points of overtime coming off high screens from center Lauri Markkanen. Though the Jazz got blown out by the Spurs Monday, the previous matchup of these teams Oct. 28, a 117-111 OT Spurs win, provided some insight as to how this Jazz team can be dangerous. Playing in their first game since the Jackson injury, George keyed a Utah comeback with a drive and layup that tied it in the final minute, and guard Brice Sensabaugh made the three that set up George's heroics, plus another three in overtime.

For the second time in a week the Mavericks face an electric scoring guard from the 2026 draft class. Sacramento's Darius Acuff's 10 of 21 performance against Dallas Monday improved his season shooting percentage to .406. Utah's Peterson, shooting 34% on the season, has shown flashes of his handle and shot creating ability, but at times has looked like a rookie trying to find his role in the offense.

Markkanen, the Jazz' other veteran big man who appears ready to win now, has been tested in Jackson's absence, chasing a 2-11 three-point shooting performance against Portland with an excellent 4-7 effort from deep against the Spurs. After disappearing for much of the second half against the Pelicans, Markkanen emerged in the final two minutes of regulation to drill a three that brought the Jazz to within one and a pair of foul shots that pushed them in front a possession later. Shouldering the load as Utah's primary frontcourt threat (starting center Jusuf Nurkic is out with a toe injury) has exposed Markkanen's strengths and flaws alike. Wednesday the Jazz produced their second 40-point quarter of the season in the third, as Markkanen and reserve center Mohamed Bamba pushed and stretched a small Pelicans lineup around the floor and the Jazz attacked the rim relentlessly. But when New Orleans went big late, Zion Williamson, Derik Queen, and Saddiq Bey all got the shots they needed against Markkanen.

Some of the Mavericks' most effective stretches against the Spurs came with PJ Washington Jr., Morez Johnson Jr., and Caleb Martin taking turns as the biggest Mavs on the floor, as Dallas' small lineup cut into the Spurs' lead even after Victor Webanyama re-entered the game. If coach Dusty May employs a similar strategy against Utah, Markkanen and Bamba will have to cover a lot of ground to keep up.

Friday's game will be the Mavericks' second of the group stage of the in-season tournament and the Jazz' first. Dallas beat Houston Friday, 116-111, to notch a 1-0 record in the group stage and a +5 point differential. Dallas trails Denver for first place in West group A, as the Nuggets' +7 point differential after their 127-120 win against Phoenix Friday gave them the tiebreaker.

Mavericks guard Walter Clayton Jr. appeared in 45 games for the Jazz last season with averages of 6.8 points and 5.5 assists before being included in the Feb. 3 trade with Memphis that brought Jaren Jackson Jr. to Utah. Jazz guard Josh Green, a Maverick fan favorite from 2020-24, comes off the bench for 3.0 points per game, and is still making things happen with hard cuts and hustle plays.

Friday's game will be shown on MAVSTV+ and KFAA Channel 29. Radio broadcast is 105.3fm KRLD (English) and 99.1fm KFZO (español).

#2747. Carmelo and La La Anthony reach divorce settlement 9 years after first splitting

Carmelo Anthony and La La Anthony (née Vázquez) reportedly have reached a settlement agreement after almost a decade-long split.

Although terms of the separation are confidential, there was a pending judgment of divorce that needed approval from the New York County Supreme Court as of Wednesday, according to People.

Once the former MTV VJ and the NBA star receive the official imprint from a judge, they'll be newly minted singles.

La La filed for divorce from the NBA star back in 2021, citing irreconcilable differences, according to TMZ, which first reported on the settlement Wednesday.

The couple began dating in 2003 after being introduced through a mutual friend, DJ Clue. They became engaged on Christmas Day 2004 and three years later welcomed their son, Kiyan Anthony, now a 19-year-old sophomore at Syracuse University, where he is playing college basketball.

The two tied the knot in July 2010 in a New York ceremony with hundreds of guests, among them sports and entertainment stars including LeBron James, Spike Lee, Serena Williams, Ciara, Kim Kardashian and Ludacris, The Times reported.

Reports of their separation surfaced in April 2017, and by August of that year, Carmelo had welcomed a daughter with ex Mia Burks.

Although the Anthonys reconciled in late 2018, they ultimately called it quits in July 2019, according to People.

La La was already using a divorce label despite it not yet being official.

In a 2022 episode of Alex Cooper's "Call Her Daddy" podcast, La La opened up about her split from Carmelo, saying that there were still difficult moments, especially regarding the co-parenting of Kiyan.

"I learned how strong I am," she said when asked about what she'd learned from the divorce. "You just find yourself getting stronger and stronger. What do they say? Like you don't know how strong you are until being strong is your only option."

La La also shared that the demise of their marriage began around the time that Carmelo was traded from the Denver Nuggets to the New York Knicks in 2011.

At the time of the 2022 interview, she shared that her perspective on love had changed. "I just don't know if it's in the cards for me," she said on the podcast.

However, in a more recent October interview on "The Jennifer Hudson Show," she revealed she was "open" to dating and that this was her "season of being open" for someone who is confident and adventurous.

As for the NBA Hall of Famer, he was rumored to be dating Racquel Smith, the widow of former NFL defensive end Will Smith. The two were seen together in June.

#2743. New Britain takes down undefeated No. 6 Southington with help from a third-quarter blocked PAT

SOUTHINGTON - The New Britain high school football mantra "slay the kings" had fallen out of fashion - or at least out of the headlines - after the Golden Hurricanes lost to reigning state champs Greenwich and New Canaan earlier this season.

It's time to dust that baby off. On Thursday night, New Britain took down Southington, the last unbeaten team in Class LL and the No. 6-ranked squad in the GametimeCT poll, 28-27 in a CCC Tier 1 showdown at Fontana Field.

This one featured big plays by the game's biggest names, yet was ultimately decided by a New Britain scout player, Javier Zenquis, who fought his way onto special teams with such dogged work in practice it often angered his teammates.

The Blue Knights can relate. Zenquis came off the edge to swat down the PAT attempt after Ben Beaulieu's second touchdown of the third quarter had closed the gap to 28-27.

At the time, it didn't seem terribly monumental. There was still 4:50 to play in the third quarter. Both teams had already put up four touchdowns apiece and there was little reason to think there wouldn't be more.

But there wasn't. Both squads buckled down with fourth-down stops in the fourth quarter, and that single point loomed larger and larger until Southington's last gasp, a fourth-and-6 pass at midfield with two minutes to play, fell incomplete.

Southington, beaten by New Britain for a third straight year, fell to 7-1. New Britain improved to 6-2 and remained in the top four of Class LL with Greenwich and Staples, as well as Southington.

"Undefeated team, phenomenal program: They're the cream of the crop here in the CCC and they were undefeated," said New Britain coach Isaiah Boddie. "We looked at it as a conference championship game."

"It was a ginormous win for us," said NB defensive end Zion Calvin. "I'm definitely grateful that we won this one."

The Golden Hurricanes never trailed Thursday. Nor could they shake the home team. Three times New Britain built leads. Three times the Blue Knights answered.

New Britain quarterback Billy Seymour's 7-yard TD run, set up by a Southington fumble on the game's opening possession, was promptly answered by a 10-yard Jacoby Roman touchdown pass to Nick Andrews.

Then came the big hits. New Britain running back Jaden Benitez broke off a 60-yard TD run down the right sideline late in the first quarter. On the first play of the second, Southington receiver Leif Renehan took a short pass from Roman and turned it into an 87-yard breakaway.

The big swing came in the final minute of the half. New Britain had taken a 21-14 lead on a 1-yard TD plunge by Benitez, but the Blue Knights had driven to the New Britain 14 and seemed poised for yet another game-tying TD.

Instead, NB linebacker Julius Mendez picked off a Roman pass in the end zone.

And though they were getting the ball to start the second half, the 'Canes weren't content to merely run out the clock. Seymour had taken long stabs downfield throughout the opening half to wide receiver Zhyair Brown. There had been some near misses. This next one did not miss. Open behind the defense, Brown pulled down a 70-yard mortar that sent NB into the break up 28-14.

"I was trying to go into the half up as many points as possible, and I knew Zhyair was down there somewhere, so I just trusted him," Seymour said. "He made a play and I couldn't be happier."

The Blue Knights punched back behind their touchdown machine from a year ago, Ben Beaulieu. The junior took a short toss on third-and-1 for a 58-yard score on Southington's first possession, then followed up a John-Michael Speight interception with a 48-yard TD in which he simply refused to go down.

Problem was, Javier Zenquis was waiting to spring. He checked with a linesman to make sure he was onside. Good thing. He wasn't. Repositioned, he made the play of the game.

"It's a game of inches, and I knew that one point makes a difference, so anything could happen," Zenquis said. "And it turns out, that's what happened."

Southington, which was playing without injured wide receiver Walker Mierzejewski, its vertical threat, will look to rebound next week against Maloney at Falcon Field. If past is prologue, the New Britain loss could be a springboard. After losing at New Britain 48-14 last year, Southington reeled off seven straight wins to reach the Class LL final.

"They're a good team, but we definitely didn't help ourselves out tonight," said Southington coach Rob Levesque. "We're going to take every ounce of the learning that needs to come out of this game and use it to our benefit. We're going to get better and fix it."

Javier Zenquis: Jaden Benitez, Billy Seymour and Zhyair Brown had the touchdowns, but Zenquis had the blocked extra point that ultimately was the difference.

"Some of the guys were getting mad at me, trying too hard on scout (team in practice). But, hey, hard work pays off and I got the block." - Javier Zenquis.

#2742. Jaguars move up in AFC standings after squashing Ravens

The Jacksonville Jaguars won on Thursday night and moved up in the AFC standings. With the Pittsburgh Steelers on a bye, the Jags' position will be at least third by the end of the weekend, and they can move into second and a tie for first place if everything goes their way.

Let's not get too far ahead of ourselves. Here are the standings as we stand now, then we will get into the rest of the weekend.

1. Buffalo Bills (6-1)2. Denver Broncos (6-2, 3-1 AFC)3. Jacksonville Jaguars (6-2, 5-2)4. Pittsburgh Steelers (6-2, 3-2 AFC)5. Kansas City Chiefs (5-2, 5-1 AFC)6. Cincinnati Bengals (5-2, 4-2 AFC)7. New England Patriots (5-3, 5-1 AFC)8. Cleveland Browns (5-3, 3-3 AFC)9. Las Vegas Raiders (4-4)10. Baltimore Ravens (4-5)11. Houston Texans (2-5)12. New York Jets (2-6, 2-3 AFC)13. Indianapolis Colts (2-6, 1-5 AFC)14. Miami Dolphins (1-6)15. Tennessee Titans (1-7)16. Los Angeles Chargers (0-7)

The Jaguars, Broncos, and Steelers all go in together and while they will all play each other eventually, that hasn't happened so we skip the head-to-head-to-head tiebreaker. The tiebreaker moves to conference record where the 3-1 Broncos best the 5-2 Jaguars and the 3-2 Steelers. Denver is the two seed.

The Broncos and Steelers haven't played each other yet, so the AFC record is applied again here and the 5-2 Jaguars slip ahead of the 3-2 Steelers. Jacksonville is the three seed and Pittsburgh is the four seed.

The Broncos can lose to the Carolina Panthers and fall to 6-3.

The Buffalo Bills, though, can't fall behind Jacksonville. The Bills could lose to the Minnesota Vikings on Monday night to fall into that 6-2 tie, but they are 5-1 in the AFC and that isn't going to change. The highest the Jaguars can get is second behind Buffalo — for now.

#2740. FA Cup memories inspiring Newport and boss Mullins

Manager Hayden Mullins and Newport County are well acquainted with the drama of the FA Cup.

Newport's famous FA Cup runs have seen giant-killing acts and games with Manchester City, Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur in the past decade.

Mullins can draw on some of his own memories of the competition heading into County's first-round tie against fellow League Two side Walsall on Saturday.

The former Crystal Palace midfielder knows better than most the magic, agony and opportunity the FA Cup can provide.

Mullins reached the Wembley showpiece with Portsmouth in 2010 after missing out on the final in Cardiff four years previously.

"I missed that final against Liverpool. I'd been sent off in the league game against them," Mullins said.

"I was told, I remember, by the manager 'no one gets sent off because if you get a straight red, you're going to miss the final.'

"And I ended up getting sent off with Luis Garcia, which wasn't my fault."

Alan Pardew's West Ham pushed Liverpool all the way and looked on course for victory, leading 3-2 deep into stoppage time at the Millennium Stadium.

But Steven Gerrard's stunning volley forced extra-time before Rafael Benitez's side eventually prevailed on penalties.

"We had a really good run with West Ham, we got to the final and we were probably a Steven Gerrard kick away from winning it," Mullins added.

"He scored one of the best goals. It dropped to him 35 yards out with cramp, and it was one of those finals where we really thought we were going to win it.

Hayden Mullins missed the 2006 FA Cup Final after he was sent off for an altercation with Liverpool's Luis Garcia. [Getty Images]

Four years later came a second shot at FA Cup glory for Mullins, this time with Portsmouth.

Playing at left-back against a star-studded Chelsea side featuring Didier Drogba, Frank Lampard, Michael Ballack and John Terry, Mullins finally got the chance to play on the biggest domestic stage.

However, silverware again eluded him as Drogba's free-kick secured a 1-0 victory for Chelsea shortly after Kevin-Prince Boateng had missed a penalty for Pompey.

Worst in the EFL - the team with a penalty problem

Those experiences have helped shape Mullins as a manager and continue to influence the culture he is building at Newport.

The County boss sees similarities between his current side and the West Ham team that reached the final in 2006.

"I can see some real similar traits in that West Ham team to what we're doing," Mullins said.

"How we were successful in that season was because we were good, dynamic and aggressive. There's some similar bits I take and try and apply when I'm working with these guys here."

Despite never lifting the trophy, Mullins' affection for the competition has only grown.

"The FA Cup has been a fantastic competition for me personally," he said.

"I grew up watching the FA Cup and for our generation one of the pinnacles was the FA Cup final.

"It's a fantastic competition. It can throw up anything so it's magical."

The competition's appeal even played a part in his decision to support Tottenhams as a boy, inspired by the club's regular cup adventures.

And that connection to north London serves as a reminder of one of Newport's most memorable FA Cup runs.

During the 2017-18 season, the Exiles beat Walsall in the first round before embarking on a remarkable journey that eventually brought Spurs to Rodney Parade.

Newport had already stunned Leeds United in round three and looked on course for one of the biggest results in the club's history when Padraig Amond put them ahead against the Premier League side in the fourth round.

But Harry Kane struck late to force a replay at Wembley - Spurs temporary home during stadium redevelopment - where a 2-0 defeat ended Mike Flynn's side's dream.

With Walsall once again drawn with Newport in round one this year, Mullins will be hoping to emulate some of Flynn's success.

"This club's got history in the cup," Mullins said.

"For any football club, a really good run in the FA Cup is always healthy. We know the revenue it generates and the eyes it puts on the players.

"It generated a lot of exposure in our groups getting to the final, so I know what this competition can do for your club but also for you personally."

And the former midfielder is well aware of the attributes a team needs for cup success.

"You've got to be a good side, you've got to ride your luck at times and you've got to be up for the game," he added.

"We've got a tough afternoon against Walsall, who are doing really well themselves, but hopefully we can come through it positively."

Why is there growing optimism at Newport County?

#2737. Ravens were down to their third QB and had a predictably ugly performance in blowout loss to Jaguars

It was sad watching the Baltimore Ravens on Thursday night.

The Ravens were a Super Bowl contender not long ago. Many thought they could bounce back from a bad year and be a top team again this season. It's a reason they were scheduled for a prime-time game against the Jacksonville Jaguars in Week 9. But Lamar Jackson got hurt early this season, then got hurt again last Sunday, and Tyler Huntley got hurt too.

That left the Ravens to play undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano, their third quarterback, on Thursday night. He played through an injured ankle and ended up having to deal with a rainstorm most of the night. He was the Ravens' only option left, and the results were predictable. The Jaguars caught the Ravens at the right time and had an easy night in a 33-10 win. The Ravens finished with 57 yards passing.

The Ravens (4-5) have decisions to make before the trade deadline. They are reportedly on the verge of dealing for Cardinals quarterback Jacoby Brissett, and while that will make them a functional offense, it's unlikely Brissett saves the season. Jackson might return from a right thumb injury but that's no guarantee, and the Ravens might be well out of the race by the time he is healed anyway.

Thursday night was an uncompetitive, bad game. The Jaguars (6-2) are clearly one of the best teams in the NFL this season, but practically any team would have defeated Baltimore on Thursday night. There wasn't anything the Ravens or Fagnano could do, no matter how many tricks they had in the game plan. It was an unwinnable situation, which might be the case for the rest of their season too.

The Ravens opened in a wildcat formation with Derrick Henry getting the first snap of the game at quarterback. There were more wildcat plays, extra linemen and any other tricks the Ravens could figure out. Henry even had a pass completion on the first drive.

No amount of trickery was saving the Ravens. The Jaguars are a good team with a strong defense and Baltimore couldn't move the ball. The rain didn't help. Baltimore had 27 yards passing in the first half. Its longest completion was 7 yards and its longest play was 9 yards in the first two quarters.

Baltimore was trying to stay in it until Jacksonville hit a big play late in the half. Against a blitz, Trevor Lawrence found Parker Washington downfield, and he was in the clear to run for a 50-yard touchdown. Lawrence had 197 passing yards in the first half, more than six times what his counterpart Fagnano had at halftime.

Washington's touchdown made the score 17-3. It's hard to count an NFL team out with a half to go, but it was hard to believe Baltimore would score 14 more points, much less outscore Jacksonville by 14.

Coming out of halftime, Ravens head coach Jesse Minter optimistically told Amazon Prime Video he wanted to see his offense score on the first drive and see what happened after that. The Ravens threw an interception on the first drive.

The Ravens were trailing 20-3 when they got a break, as Travis Hunter fumbled and Baltimore recovered near midfield. But the Ravens couldn't get a first down, and on fourth-and-inches tight end Mark Andrews, lined up for what looked like a tush push, fumbled the snap. It looked like he was going to turn and hand it off but it didn't matter because he couldn't hold onto the ball.

It was that kind of night. The Jaguars caused some of those issues too. Their defense is very good, and the offense is capable of putting up a lot of points if there's not a downpour of rain. They have a good chance of making a deep playoff run.

The same could have been said about the Ravens before Jackson's latest injury. Brissett will be an upgrade over what we saw against the Jaguars, but there was a reason he was demoted to third string by Arizona this week and then was available in a trade. The Ravens' season probably isn't going anywhere. Things could look even worse in Baltimore by Tuesday's trade deadline.

Per ESPN's Jamison Hensley, this is the first time in the Ravens' 31-year history they've lost three straight games by at least 20 points. They at least get a long rest before "Monday Night Football" against the Los Angeles Chargers next week, at which point trade acquisition Jacoby Brissett should be ready to go.

Somehow, the game wasn't as close as the score made it look. The Jaguars finish off a beatdown of a Ravens team starting its last resort at quarterback.

Trevor Lawrence had a few moments of brilliance, and that was all Jacksonville needed to make this game one-sided from the start.

Joe Fagnano isn't thriving, but he isn't quitting either. He scrambles and makes a guy miss to convert a 3rd-and-9.

That 3-yard run brings Justice Hill up to 77 on the night. He got 65 of those on a single run, but that's still enough to break a 24-game streak of the Jaguars defense not allowing a 75-yard rusher, assuming he doesn't lose any of those yards.

A Raven somehow broke that streak in this game, and it wasn't Derrick Henry.

And now a 3-and-out for the Jaguars, who punt it to the Ravens' 13-yard line.

Justice Hill gets a little dignity back with a 65-yard touchdown run. That at least perked up what remains of the crowd.

Chris Rodriguez Jr. punches it in from two yards out on a direct snap. 7:26 to go in a classic "sim to end" game.

The Ravens' last three drives have ended in turnovers while gaining nine yards total. This is some impressively awful football.

Looks like the Ravens are about to lose a fumble on the kickoff return. The Jaguars challenge after LeJohntay Wester was ruled down by contact and replay makes it look like they will win it.

The Jaguars have gained 50 yards total since halftime. That's all they've needed to put this game well out of reach with 11:52 remaining.

Jourdan Lewis picks off Joe Fagnano at the Baltimore 23 and the Jaguars are probably about to score again.

Fagnano is 9-for-17 for 46 yards, 0 touchdowns and 2 interceptions. Expectations were low tonight and, well, the offense has acted accordingly.

Cam Little is good from 47 after the drive stalls out. Carry on.

The good news for the Ravens is Kyle Hamilton is on the sideline and doesn't seem to be in any distress. So that might just be a "why would we risk this" type of ruling out.

#2736. Alexander Ovechkin announces this will be his last NHL season: 'Let's have fun'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

Carr, the Lakers' first-round pick out of Baylor, is incredibly athletic but is raw, which is why he has played in a total of four minutes across three games. He needs to be down in the G League just to get some run.

#2734. ‘We actually need’: Paul George tells Boston Celtics teammate he needs to do more

Paul George has had a great start to life with the Boston Celtics, but the same can't be said about every new player in the franchise.

The Celtics signed Mitchell Robinson as a free agent after his championship-winning season with the New York Knicks, and a lot was expected of him.

Unfortunately, Robinson has not done enough yet, and George has had his say on the situation.

Robinson has played in seven of the Boston Celtics' eight games so far this season, but he has not hit the heights he was expected to.

The 28-year-old has only managed double-digit points in one fixture, and in four of the seven games, he scored under five points. There has also been a drop-off in his rebounds, assists, steals and blocks compared to previous seasons.

That has led to some frustration among the Celtics fan base, and George has admitted that his new teammate has to do a little bit more.

However, the former Philadelphia 76ers star is convinced that Robinson will come good and has offered him complete support.

He told CLNS: "I think it was a different situation for him in New York to here, where we actually need him to do a little bit more and want him to do a little bit more and kind of explore that.

"He's just going through that. It's a different play style for him. He'll get there. For me as well, I'm still learning and still figuring out. But I have no doubt. He's got a high IQ, he plays hard. I think it's just an adjustment.

"I'm still trying to figure it out myself. We're all in this together. The biggest thing about it is that he knows that we're here for him. We're all collectively here to help him through this. It's not a thing that he has to navigate on his own.

"So, just with that, I think he's starting to explore just what game and who he is here for us."

Robinson was never really going to be a superstar for the Celtics, but he still hasn't done enough for them since moving to Boston in the summer.

George only joined in the off-season too, but he has been fantastic. That should serve as motivation for the former Knicks star going forward.

#2730. 49ers’ George Kittle pleads the 5th on Brandon Aiyuk’s expected return to facility

49ers' George Kittle pleads the 5th on Brandon Aiyuk's expected return to facility appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Brandon Aiyuk is reportedly inching closer to making a return to the NFL, after last having played in October 2024. Aiyuk suffered a torn ACL, MCL and meniscus injuries in his right knee against the Kansas City Chiefs, and now plans to return to the 49ers' training facility.

And well, tight end George Kittle hilariously declined to discuss Aiyuk's potential return to the team, per a post on X by Grant Cohn.

"Plead the fifth, yeah. You can ask John. Or Kyle. Don't ask me. I'm a conspiracy guy," he said.

Kittle's response came as Aiyuk's agent, Drew Rosenhaus, confirmed Wednesday that the 28-year-old had submitted the necessary paperwork to return and planned to report to the 49ers' facility Friday afternoon. Rosenhaus said Aiyuk was healthy and ready to play, and San Francisco will now determine whether to reinstate Aiyuk.

General Manager John Lynch describing the situation as fluid and confirmed that the organization is working with the NFL Management Council to find a path that works for both sides, per ESPN. Head coach Kyle Shanahan said he had mentally moved on from Aiyuk and did not expect an immediate resolution.

Aiyuk missed the entire 2025 season during his recovery. His relationship with San Francisco deteriorated further after the organization voided approximately $27 million in guaranteed contract money in July 2025, citing his failure to complete required rehabilitation sessions.

The 49ers subsequently placed him on the reserve/left squad list in December after he stopped reporting to the facility, and his failure to report for training camp in July resulted in his placement on the reserve/did not report list. His current designation means San Francisco is not paying him and he does not occupy a spot on the active roster.

The 49ers have previously attempted to trade Aiyuk, and a release remains a likely outcome.

#2728. Three reasons why the Brewers can repeat as World Series champions in 2027

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Milwaukee Brewers are the freshly crowned World Series champions for 2026. Add that trophy to a regular season body of work in which they won 103 games and achieved the best run differential in all of Major League Baseball, and it's clear the Brewers this season did all a team can do. The first title in franchise history will be remembered and cherished by the Brewers and their fans forever, and it was earned in every respect.

The celebrations won't soon end, and the post-Game 5 hangovers are still pulsing. Even so, it's time to turn our attention to the 2027 season and explore why the Brewers absolutely have the foundation necessary to do it all again next year. Here, then, are three reasons the Brewers can become repeat champions roughly one year from now.

Eyeball the Brewers' current contract obligations and service time tiers, and you'll find just six players are likely bound for free agency. Brandon Woodruff, Jake Bauers, JoJo Romero, and Gary Sánchez will be free agents soon. Elsewhere, Dustin May has a mutual option for 2027, which means he'll probably join them. Finally, Antonio Senzatela has a $14 million team option for 2027 on which the Brewers may pass.

Of those, the 31-year-old Bauers is the biggest needle-mover, as he's coming off a 2026 season in which he hit 26 home runs in 144 games and put up a WAR of 3.3. He does seem likely to move on, but the Brewers are more than resourceful enough to find comparable production from the non-premium position of first base.

Elsewhere, the Brewers should resist the temptation to trade away catcher, linchpin, and reigning World Series MVP William Contreras ahead of his walk year in 2027. The Brewers Way in recent years has been to part ways with core contributors around such a time, and that may be a temptation with Contreras, especially given Bo Naylor's presence on the roster. Contreras, though, is not easily replaceable given his skills behind the mask and his high level of production at the plate. An extension may not be something the Brewers will pursue – even though the ongoing CBA negotiations will probably lead to a new system that benefits teams like Milwaukee – but even if that's the case, they should keep their catcher and leader around for the final year of team control in the name of defending the belt and the title.

The champion Brewers, as a club that gets limited investment from ownership and is elite at player development, skews young even as they stand as the best team in baseball. Consider:

As for specific examples, they're not hard to find. Budding star Jackson Chourio will be in his age-23 campaign in 2027. Jacob Misiorowski and Logan Henderson will each be 25. Cooper Pratt, like Chourio, will be 23. The Brewers this past season got 16.4 WAR from those names, and Pratt and Henderson didn't even log full seasons.

Let's also note that Brice Turang, who led the Brewers this season with a WAR of 7.3, will be just 27 in '27 and thus should continue performing at a high level. This isn't just a matter of the Brewers being largely shielded from age-related decline next season. There's also the distinct possibility that so many of their 2026 pace-setters are still pre-prime and may have even better days ahead.

As though all of the above weren't enough, the Brewers right now have managed to thread this rare needle: they're the best team at the highest level and have one of the best collections of talent down on the farm. MLB.com in August ranked the Brewers as the third-best farm system in the game right now. FanGraphs ranked them third based on average prospect value. Baseball America at midseason likewise ranked the Milwaukee system third and after the season gave the system an "A" grade.

At an individual level, a number of premium Brewers prospects figure to arrive at some point next season. That list includes shortstop Jesús Made, who may be the top prospect in the game right now. Other 2027 arrivals may include talents like corner infielder Andrew Fischer, right-handers Tyson Hardin and Bishop Letson, and infielder/outfielder Jett Williams, among others. So many teams in contending mode have a fairly dry pipeline thanks to the low draft picks and the now-for-later trades that often accompany World Series aspirations, but that's very much not the case with lead executive Matt Arnold and the Brewers.

Celebrations of the work done in 2026 should be the focus right now for the Crew and their rooters, and once that dies down, they can all be further buoyed by the reality that the Brewers aren't going anywhere. The guess here is that the Brewers open the 2027 season – whatever it looks like — as the consensus favorites to do it all again.

That said, the Red Sox have a crowded outfield with Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, and Roman Anthony, which means a Duran swap may be needed to clear the decks. Potential fits: Phillies, Cubs, Mariners, Rangers

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 50%

Hernández has been a reliable power presence for the Dodgers, but now, at age 34, he's been showing some signs of decline. On another level, the Dodgers want to make space for elite prospect Josue De Paula to receive regular playing time, and there aren't any other paths to it. That may mean Hernández will be on the move.

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 45%

Kwan's another who's been a reliable presence in the trade rumors for some time. Cleveland also has a history of dealing core talents leading up to their walk year, and Kwan is indeed slated for free agency after next season. The timing would be right, as Kwan is coming off a 5.0-WAR season for the second time in his career.

Potential fits: Phillies, Blue Jays, Cubs, Mariners

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 30%

McClanahan's long and labored comeback from Tommy John surgery was finally realized this past season, and he turned in a strong age-29 campaign for the Rays. These, though, are the Rays, and McClanahan's forthcoming arbitration payday combined with his uncertain health history may prompt them to shop him to pitching-starved fellow contenders. He carries risk, of course, but there will no doubt be potential takers lining up for him.

Potential fits: Braves, Padres, Orioles, Tigers

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 35%

Thanks to a blazing fastball and wipeout knuckle curve, the soon-to-be 33-year-old Megill has been a lockdown closer for most of the last three seasons. The Brewers of course have a substantial history of trading away closers before they reach their high-salary years and also before they regress/decline (see: Hader, Josh and Williams, Devin). That could again be the case with Megill, who'll be in line for free agency after the 2027 season.

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 55%

He's the most dominant closer in baseball and the owner of one of the biggest fastballs ever, and he's under team control through the 2029 season. So why would the contending Padres trade Miller at the peak of his powers? They'd consider doing so because they have a lot of roster holes to fill elsewhere, especially with Michael King opting out of his contract. Trading away Miller would in theory allow them to fill some of those holes, which is why it'll be a temptation for lead executive AJ Preller. No doubt, fellow contenders will be lining up if the Pads do indeed shop the NL saves leader.

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 20%

Strider not so long ago was in the discussion for most dominant starter in the bigs, but persistent arm woes have turned him into a question mark. The Braves came close to dealing Strider at the deadline in exchange for more of a known quantity in the rotation, so there's basis for his inclusion on this list. Any team acquiring him will have to be comfortable with Strider's medicals and the fact that he's owed a minimum of $49 million over the next two seasons. His ace upside, though, is surely tantalizing.

Potential fits: Cardinals, Padres, Orioles, Tigers, Dodgers

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 25%

The Nats were clear sellers at the deadline, but they retained Abrams, who has two full years of team control remaining. In other words, it's going to take a lot to pry him away. At 26, he's coming off a 30-30 season, and he's been a quite productive bat over the last three years. Defensively, Abrams probably isn't an everyday shortstop moving forward, but second base is now in his toolkit.

Potential fits: Braves, Pirates, Red Sox, Giants, Rangers

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 25%

Teams will pay a lot for a young and controllable starting pitcher with frontline upside, and all of that describes the 27-year-old lefty Detmers. Not eligible for free agency until after the 2028 season, Detmers topped 4.0 WAR this past season and struck out 211 batters in 185 innings. For the Halos, trading him might be an example of selling high.

Potential fits: Cardinals, Red Sox, Cubs, Blue Jays, Padres

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 30%

As a 27-year-old All-Star catcher with three full seasons of team control remaining, Goodman would cost a lot in trade. Perhaps that's why the rebuilding Rockies will indeed deal him this winter. There's no doubt that playing his home games in Coors Field helps Goodman's cause, but this past season, he was actually much more productive on the road. Away from Coors, he hit 25 of his 41 home runs in 2026, and his road slugging percentage was .564 versus a .490 figure at a mile above sea level. That's power that will play anywhere.

Potential fits: Giants, White Sox, Yankees, Orioles

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 50%

Greene has one of the biggest fastballs in the game and a top 10 finish in the NL Cy Young balloting in his recent past. However, he's struggled to stay healthy and realize his potential on a sustained basis – the potential that made him the No. 2 overall draft pick in 2017. He's signed through 2028 with a club option for 2029, and it may be time for a change of scenery. He's been the subject of trade speculation before.

Potential fits: Dodgers, Braves, Red Sox, Astros, Blue Jays

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 25%

Herrera is not a particularly skilled defensive catcher outside of blocking pitches in the dirt, but he can get by behind the mask, at least on a part-time basis. He also has a plus bat, which will play at DH or perhaps first base and even left field. The Cardinals have an incoming glut of catchers, which means it may be time to move on from Herrera. He's not eligible for free agency until after the 2029 season.

Potential fits: Yankees, White Sox, Orioles, Giants

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 30%

The Marlins seem likely to trade away one of their middle infielders this winter, either the shortstop Lopez or second baseman Xavier Edwards. For now, we'll focus on Lopez, who would likely fetch the higher return. The 28-year-old Lopez this past season topped 6.0 WAR, led the NL in hits, and swiped 34 bases, all while grading out as a valuable defender at the premium position of short. He's under team control through the 2029 season, which means he'll have immense trade value.

Potential fits: Braves, Phillies, Red Sox, Rays

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 20%

The most underrated player in baseball? The 25-year-old Neto is very much in that discussion. Over the last three seasons, he's amassed a WAR of 15.6, which puts him in elite territory. Any team in need of excellence and stability on the left side of the infield should have interest. Neto isn't eligible for free agency until after the 2029 season, which adds to his already substantial trade value.

Potential fits: Braves, Red Sox, Tigers, Cardinals, Yankees

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 30%

No, this one isn't likely to happen, as Contreras has proved central to the Brewers' success in 2026 and for years prior. That said, the ever-resourceful Brewers do have a ready replacement on the roster in Bo Naylor. The 2026 World Series MVP is also in line for free agency after the 2027 season, which theoretically increases the chances that Milwaukee will explore his trade market. Speaking of which, such a skilled catcher with a potent bat and reputation as a leader will indeed have a healthy market.

Potential fits: Yankees, Rangers, Orioles

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 15%

For years now, it seems, we've been waiting for the Mariners to trade from their surfeit of starting pitching. They moved Luis Castillo at the deadline, but perhaps this time, they finally flip one of their big guns. Gilbert, 29, will be a pending free agent in 2027, which straightaway makes him a trade candidate for a Mariners club that's more averse to spending than they should be. He's an attractive one, too, as Gilbert has been a reliable source of innings over his career to date, and he also boasts a 3.58 FIP and a sparkling 5.14 K/BB ratio over the last four seasons.

Potential fits: Mets, Braves, Orioles, Cubs, White Sox

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 45%

Paredes, who turns 28 in February, is on a $13.35 million team option for 2027, and then he's eligible for free agency. That adds up to the real possibility of a trade out of Houston. While there are questions as to how Paredes' bat will play without the Crawford Boxes near at hand, there's no doubt he's overall a valuable performer. He's fresh off a 4.0-WAR season in 2026 and relatively young as notable trade targets go.

Potential fits: Phillies, Cardinals, Yankees

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 45%

Peña, like Paredes, will be a pending free agent in 2027, and the increasingly incompetent Astros may look to trade him as they did Kyle Tucker back in the winter of 2024-25. Peña, 29, hasn't been especially durable over the last two seasons, but when on the field, he remains an excellent all-around performer. If he is indeed shopped, then he's the most appealing shortstop on the trade and free agent markets this offseason.

Potential fits: Braves, Red Sox, Phillies

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 35%

Ryan has been the subject of trade speculation for what feels like the last half-decade. Has the time finally come for those rumors to be realized? Now 30, Ryan will be a free agent after the 2027 season, and that of course means he could be on the move this winter. He has excellent stuff, and over the last three seasons Ryan boasts an ERA+ of 117 and a K/BB ratio of 5.38.

Potential fits: Cubs, Astros, Mets, Orioles, Red Sox, Blue Jays

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 35%

Yes, deGrom is 38, but going into the final guaranteed year of his contract, he remains capable of being a solid rotation presence for a contender. deGrom reportedly used his full no-trade clause to block a trade to the Braves at the deadline, so it's far from certain whether he'd be willing to approve a deal out of Arlington. That said, such things are always negotiations, and a late-career run at the playoffs might prove tempting for him.

Potential fits: Braves, Dodgers, Blue Jays

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 25%

The future Hall of Famer is coming off another solid season once you consider that a spring hamate injury likely sapped his production early on. That said, he soon turns 33, and he's still owed $160 million through 2031. That's in addition to his full no-trade clause. The Mets and Lindor, though, may be at a crossroads in their relationship, which makes it at least theoretically possible that a change of scenery is in the offing.

Potential fits: Braves, Mariners, Phillies

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 15%

Marte already had a partial no-trade clause in his contract, which runs through 2030 (with a 2031 player option), and now he's earned a full no-trade clause through 10-and-5 rights. That said, after multiple somewhat bizarre AWOL incidents with the D-backs, Marte and the club may be looking for a fresh start. While Marte's offensive outputs dipped last season, his age-32 campaign, he still profiles as at least an above-average player for the near- to mid-term. And he may be more than that if he gets back to something like his pre-2026 peak.

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 30%

Now 32, Seager will always have health and durability concerns, but he remains a plus defensive shortstop who produces well at the plate by positional standards. With the Rangers perhaps looking to shed payroll, they could seek to move Seager, who's owed another $155 million through the 2031 season. As with the Mets and Lindor, that may mean kicking in cash to make a trade happen, but Seager would help the cause for any contender in need of help at the shortstop position.

Potential fits: Braves, Mariners, Phillies

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 20%

Will the increasingly listless Reds pivot toward a longer-term rebuild? If they do, then their electric 24-year-old shortstop could be dangled. De La Cruz is coming off his best season to date, and there's the feeling that he still has offensive upside in the tank. He's under team control through the 2029 season. Those three full years of control plus De La Cruz's MVP upside mean we'd be talking about a true blockbuster of a trade. No, it's not particularly likely to happen, but it's an intriguing possibility.

Chances he'll be traded (wild guess): 15%

This is becoming something of an annual exercise in speculation and wish-casting (wish-casting by non-Pirates fans, anyway). Skenes took a step back last season in terms of run prevention and underlying indicators, and he also lost a bit off his fastball. Still, he was overall a high-value pitcher who still projects as an ace, and he's not far removed from those legendary rookie and sophomore seasons. Like De La Cruz above, Skenes has three more full seasons before free agency, which makes his trade value pretty well stratospheric. The Pirates aren't likely at all to move him, particularly ahead of a new CBA that may benefit teams of their sort, but the Skenes trade conjecture isn't going anywhere.
